#1000. Adames to fight Warburton on November 14 live on Sky Sports

Carlos Adames will fight Gerome Warburton as part of Riyadh Season Zuffa Boxing 13 on November 14, live on Sky Sports; a 10-round bantamweight co-feature will see Jason 'Mayhem' Moloney make his Zuffa Boxing debut against Andres Teran

WBC middleweight world champion Carlos Adames will fight Welsh southpaw Gerome Warburton on Saturday, November 14, live on Sky Sports.

The pair meet in a 10-round main event of Riyadh Season Zuffa Boxing 13, with the bout to be contested at a contract weight of 165 pounds.

Adames, 25-1-1 (18), returns to action less than eight months after his dominant win over Austin 'Ammo' Williams, the third title defence for the Dominican Republic native, who is unbeaten in his last eight bouts.

Warburton, 18-2-2 (2), reignited his career in 2026, earning back-to-back decision victories over former British middleweight champion Nathan Heaney.

The 31-year-old from Colwyn Bay, Wales, is a former Welsh middleweight champion who has challenged for British and Commonwealth honors.

The 10-round bantamweight co-feature will see Australian former world champion Jason 'Mayhem' Moloney, 29-4 (20), make his Zuffa Boxing debut against Mexico's Andres Teran, 19-2 (14).

Moloney, a consensus world-ranked contender, has won two consecutive bouts in Australia to position himself for another championship run. Teran turned heads at Zuffa Boxing 08 in June, knocking out the previously undefeated Floyd Diaz in the sixth round.

Also fighting on November 14, super-middleweight contender Bruno Surace, two fights since his knockout victory over Jaime Munguia, takes on Poland's unbeaten Kamil Bednarek in a 10-rounder.

In an eight-round tilt featuring unbeaten lightweights, Mexico's Ivan Ortiz will battle Dariial Kuchmenov.

#999. Asian Cup postponed following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The 24-team tournament was due to kick off in January but has been moved back to at least December 2027

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The 2027 Asian Cup has been postponed by almost up to a year following recent attacks on hosts Saudi Arabia, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has confirmed.

The tournament, which was due to kick-off on January 7, has been rescheduled due to “exceptional circumstances”, the AFC said.

In October, a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement claiming responsibility.

The AFC said the 24-team tournament could now take place from December 23 next year to January 21, 2028.

"The new dates of the tournament will be presented to Fifa for approval," the AFC said.

“Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

Several Premier League players, including Aston Villa’s Japan international goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, Manchester City’s Uzbekistan international defender Abdukodir Khusanov and Hull City’s Australia international defender Lucas Herrington, would have had to leave their clubs mid-season to take part in the tournament but will now be available for their teams this season.

Disruptions in travel and security concerns have affected other sporting events in Saudi Arabia, ‌with the Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has been moved from October to December. Not all sport in the region ‌has been called off, however, with Saul "Canelo" ​Alvarez beating Christian Mbilli in their world title bout in Riyadh on Saturday.

Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice is a player Mikel Arteta dare not substitute, and was the difference at Anfield once more in an ever-impressive run, writes Henry Winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In what was inevitably a hugely competitive Ballon d’Or in a World Cup year, some exceptional talents were always going to miss out on votes.

Arsenal won the most demanding title in the world, the Premier League, and fought their way to the Champions League final. They boasted eight players who reached the semi-finals of the World Cup, and three Spaniards who won it, yet Arsenal’s highest-ranked player in the Ballon d’Or was only 15th - Declan Rice. Frustration at that lack of recognition may provide further fuel driving them through this season.

As one of the Ballon d’Or judges, I was determined to cast a vote for Rice, even if it meant only one point in placing him 10th. The excellence of Rice’s season deserved acknowledgement. He should have been named Footballer of the Year by the writers, and he certainly got my vote, but our industry plumped for Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes, who’s grabbing headlines for different reasons now.

I backed Rice because he’s a winner. The three criteria that the Ballon d’Or organisers, France Football, tell us to adhere to are essentially individual performance, collective performance (i.e. trophies) and role model qualities. (It’s why Harry Kane won overall).

Rice delivered on all counts, and he continues this season, registering five assists already from midfield, targeting further glory with Arsenal defending their title, and playing the game the right way. Rice doesn’t dive. He’d get in any midfield, barring possibly Paris Saint-Germain’s.

The best compliment that can be paid to Arsenal’s box-to-box destroyer and assist-maker is that he looks increasingly the natural midfield heir to Patrick Vieira, captain of the club’s greatest team, the Invincibles of 2003/04. In Sunday’s demanding game at Anfield with the stakes high, and the pressure even higher, Rice again rose to the occasion. He put in a pacey, well-timed overlap and cross for Kai Havertz’s goal, and then provided constant, mobile resistance when Liverpool threatened.

He’s a no.6, increasingly a no.8, who has responded to Mikel Arteta’s pre-season encouragement to attack more. He combines elite technique and temperament. He showed his quick feet to whisk the ball around Florian Wirtz, used his right foot to create Havertz’s goal, and then his left foot to ping a pass down the line to Havertz. He twice closed down Bradley Barcola. He toyed with Ronald Araujo before crossing to Noni Madueke.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

He is now, unquestionably, Arsenal’s most important player, especially with Bukayo Saka struggling for sustained fitness. He’s surely the eventual successor to Martin Odegaard as captain. The club are currently looking to tie Rice, 27, down to the most significant contract of his career, taking him through his peak years.

He’s so important that Arteta dare not take him off. Rice completed 90 minutes in the win against Liverpool, in the draw against Bayern Munich when he scored at the Allianz, in the victory at Napoli, the home win over Leeds United and away win at Nottingham Forest. He played all but five minutes of the triumph at Aston Villa.

That also stirs concern around the vexed issue of over-playing. Rice endured neural pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season. The England international did have a three-week rest when withdrawing from consideration for the last international break. Thomas Tuchel will doubtless want his most powerful midfielder returning for the forthcoming Nations League games against Croatia at Wembley and away to Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid.

Only a mathematical meltdown – an 8-0 loss to Croatia - would deny England qualification to the Nations League quarter-finals. England will want to overhaul Spain, and finish top of Group A3, ensuring they play a runner-up in March (the semi-finals and final are June 9-13), so Tuchel is likely to go strong. There will inevitably be some club managers hoping their players are rested.

That is a conversation for Tuchel and Arteta to have. Rice always wants to represent England, adding to his 80 caps. He’s currently joint 22nd in the all-time appearance list with Gary Lineker, and would climb into the top 20, past Rio Ferdinand and alongside Raheem Sterling, if he features against Croatia and Spain.

He has so much to offer club and country.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'

#997. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

#995. Penrice handed first Scotland call as McTominay returns

James Penrice has impressed since joining Rangers on loan from AEK Athens; Scott McTominay and Che Adams return from injury; Blackburn's Kristi Montgomery keeps his place; Scotland host North Macedonia on November 13 with final Nations League game away to Switzerland three days later

Football Journalist @AlisonGConroy

James Penrice has been handed his first Scotland call-up with Scott McTominay returning for their crucial Nations League double-header against North Macedonia and Switzerland.

Rangers defender Penrice has impressed since joining on loan from AEK Athens and is called up in place of the injured Josh Doig.

McTominay is recalled after missing the last camp due to minor heart surgery. Since returning the 29-year-old has started the past seven matches for Napoli, scoring four goals.

Torino striker Che Adams also returns after missing Sebastien Pocognoli's first squad with a thigh strain.

Blackburn's Kristi Montgomery keeps his place after being drafted in to replace Kenny McLean in the last squad. The Norwich midfielder remains out, although Celtic's Kieran Tierney returns.

Dinamo Zagreb defender Scott McKenna, who played three out of the four games in the group before being sent off in the win against North Macedonia, is out injured. There is no place for Celtic's Colby Donovan this time as Pocognoli cuts his squad to 26 from 28.

If Andy Robertson plays the next two Scotland matches, he will move on to 103 appearances and become the country's most capped player, surpassing Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Scotland must take at least four points from their final two games in League B1 to have a chance of even finishing second.

They also need Slovenia to drop points against North Macedonia and Switzerland to have a chance of reaching the promotion play-offs.

Relegation to League C is also still a possibility if they lose their first game at Hampden Park.

"We have a list of players, like I said in my first camp, that we select regarding the performance in the clubs. But also the style of play or the way that we want to play. We have some missing players around the left side.

"We have plenty of experience back in the squad, with Scott [McTominay], with Che [Adams] and with Kieran [Tierney], who is also back.

A 14-year-old boy has been arrested on suspicion of a public order offence and bailed after a Coventry supporter appeared to mock Sunderland fans over the death of Bradley Lowery during the Premier League match between the sides on Saturday.

Sunderland fan Lowery captured the hearts of the football world during his battle with neuroblastoma – a rare and aggressive type of childhood cancer. He died at the age of six in 2017.

A video emerged on Saturday of a young supporter in the home end holding up a picture of Lowery on his phone and pointing to the screen while smirking. He was holding the screen towards the Sunderland fans in the away end.

A West Midlands Police statement on Tuesday said: “A teenage boy arrested on suspicion of a public order offence in Coventry has been bailed with conditions.”

Police confirmed on Sunday that a 14-year-old boy had handed himself in while they investigated the incident, which took place at the Coventry Building Society Arena during Saturday’s 3-1 win.

Lowery’s mother, Gemma, issued a statement through the Bradley Lowery Foundation on Sunday. She said her “beautiful boy” Bradley “deserves to be remembered with love, not hate”.

“To see such a beautiful memory used in such a cruel way really does make my heart hurt,” she added. “We are a football-loving family who follow Sunderland home and away. I’m all for football banter, but surely mocking a child who died from cancer is not banter?

“I hope the club takes appropriate action and the young lad’s family help him understand how hurtful his actions were. I don’t want hatred directed towards him, so please please don’t, just for him to learn from this.”

In their statement on Sunday, West Midlands Police had added: “We understand the upset and outrage this video has caused in the community and to the victim’s family and our officers are keeping them up to date with the progress of our investigation and working closely alongside both football clubs.”

Coventry said they were aware of the social media footage and added: “The club does not tolerate offensive behaviour and will liaise with the relevant authorities to determine the appropriate course of action.”

Fortress Anfield is no more. Arsenal proved Liverpool have lost their fear factor.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool certainly didn’t lack effort or endeavour in their 1-0 defeat to Arsenal at Anfield, and were denied a clear penalty for Jurrien Timber’s shirt pull on Alexander Isak in the first half, but another home defeat underlines where Andoni Iraola’s side must improve.

For the Reds’ new Spanish boss, the 90 minutes against Mikel Arteta’s defensively-excellent side showed exactly where Liverpool are at in their development.

The headline stat of zero Opta-defined shots on target for the home side for the first time since records began in 2003 tells the story in more way than one.

Liverpool’s attack struggled against Arteta’s team that thrives defensively, especially when going a goal ahead early in the game.

It was that early part of the game that Iraola chose to focus on post-match, saying: “Overall, I think we have to blame especially the start of the game and until we conceded the goal. I think the start hasn't been at the level of the game.”

Liverpool recovered well, but breaking down the champions who are more than happy to sit on a 1-0 lead and defend like a prime Tony Pulis or Sam Allardyce-drilled side is a thankless task.

It gets results, even more so when their tactic of delaying any momentum being built by the opposition is so easily bought by the referee.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

No wonder Virgil van Dijk admitted post-match that he shared Liverpool fans’ frustration at the fouls being awarded every time a Liverpool player went near a man in an Arsenal shirt.

“I got a card towards the end, so I probably shared it as well," the Dutchman said.

But for all the frustration at Arsenal’s antics and the referee’s inability to see through it, Liverpool’s front three of Isak, Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola simply have to offer more if they are to win games like these.

Barcola doesn’t look adjusted to this level of fixture in the Premier League yet. The Frenchman certainly puts in the work off the ball and contests plenty of duels (losing 12 of the 18 he contested), but going forward more will be needed from the £123 million signing.

The reality is that this front three of Isak, Gakpo and Barcola - signed for a combined sum just shy of £300m - are currently a far-cry from the Firmino, Salah, Mane trio that combined physical presence with quality output. Opposition defences certainly don't fear this new-look attack the way they did previously.

Florian Wirtz, in the No. 10 role behind the front three, was a busy presence, frequently the available option to play out and find pockets of space, and never shying away from the difficult task of playing in that area of the pitch against this Arsenal side. Again, though, he was signed to be the player to unlock such defences.

Liverpool did have 17 attempts on goal and 48 touches inside Arsenal’s box, but the final pass or finish wasn’t there.

And while Arsenal aren’t an easy team to open up, finding ways to do so is what’s required if you are to compete at the top and win the big games. Sunday afternoon marked Arsenal’s first win at Anfield in 14 years.

Iraola knows where his side must improve, having scored the fewest goals of the teams in the top seven of the table after nine games played, saying: “I think we've had a lot of situations inside the box – not even around the box, inside the box – that definitely we haven't finished properly.”

When Liverpool are next at Anfield it’s the visit of Manchester United after the international break, by which point the Reds will have won one home league game in almost seven months. Of course, that spans the end of Arne Slot’s tenure, the summer, and two international breaks, but one win from five home league matches for Iraola is far from ideal.

Much is made of ‘Fortress Anfield’ but for the past two seasons that has been far from the case. Last season, the Reds failed to win nine of their 19 home league games. Failing to win 47% of your home games isn’t going to get you anywhere near the title. This season, albeit five games in, it’s 20%. Teams no longer fear coming to Anfield.

Last year, Man United registered their first win at Anfield since 2016. Forest, who recorded consecutive wins at Anfield for the first time since the 1960s, are now three unbeaten at Anfield. It’s a similar story for Manchester City, winning their last two visits after going 23 years without doing so, with fans in attendance.

It’s not just the big clubs who have come away from Anfield unscathed; Fulham, Sunderland, Leeds, Burnley and Brentford in the last year have all collected points.

And therein lies the issue, if Liverpool can’t find ways to break down teams that play defensively at Anfield, they will struggle to compete for the title. In their five home games this season they’ve scored just four goals - their lowest since 2012.

Iraola, of course, knows this, and he has also acknowledged the need to get the crowd onside and how important it is to start games well in order to do so.

It’s clear where Liverpool need to improve, so the Kop can chant ‘Attack, Attack, Attack’ again.

Matt Ladson is the co-founder and editor of This Is Anfield, the independent Liverpool news and comment website, and covers all areas of the Reds for FourFourTwo – including transfer analysis, interviews, title wins and European trophies. As well as writing about Liverpool for FourFourTwo he also contributes to other titles including Yahoo and Bleacher Report. He is a lifelong fan of the Reds.

#991. Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why

Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Few national elections carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.

Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.

"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.

"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."

The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.

During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.

Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.

"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest,'" said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Center at London-based think tank Chatham House.

"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.

"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.

More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.

In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".

"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.

"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.

#990. Carragher: Boring Newcastle face a tough season ahead

Newcastle were booed off at home after losing 1-0 to Everton on Monday Night Football; Matthias Jaissle's side have lost three of their last four Premier League matches; Newcastle are 13th with three wins from nine games and head to Fulham, who are below them, on Saturday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jamie Carragher described Newcastle as 'flat and boring' following their defeat to Everton on Monday Night Football and reckons Matthias Jaissle's side face a difficult season.

Thierno Barry's second-half goal earned Everton a 1-0 win at St James' Park and their first away victory in the Premier League this season, as Newcastle were booed off at half-time and full-time following their fourth defeat in five games across all competitions.

Newcastle have slipped to 13th and are four points above the bottom three, with a trip to lowly Fulham to come on Saturday.

"It is going to be a tough season for them," said Carragher. "I felt tonight [Monday] was actually more important for Newcastle than the cup game [Carabao Cup loss at Everton last week], and it was the other way round for Everton, who are desperate for a trophy.

"But I fear a little bit for Newcastle, it could be a long, tough season."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jaissle was appointed in August, replacing Eddie Howe, and made a promising start by earning entertaining draws against Liverpool and Bournemouth, with a win at Tottenham sandwiched in between, but that has quickly faded as their home form has continued to be an issue.

No Premier League side have lost more home games in 2026 than Newcastle (7) and they have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their last 14 games at St James' Park, the longest run in their league history.

Carragher added: "Watching them of late, especially at home, it feels flat and a little bit boring, and that was one thing I didn't think I'd ever be describing Jaissle's Newcastle as.

"You think of the system he's come from, the Red Bull model, how they like to play. At times, those types of teams and managers can leave themselves open at the back, but it's front-footed, it's aggressive, it's getting the crowd involved, and we've just never seen any of that at all tonight. I'm a little bit flummoxed watching it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I was really impressed with him, how he came across. They were very impressive at Spurs, a great result for them early on, and the results in the main have been okay, but there's always been a worry about the performances and their underlying numbers, even early on.

"I watched Fulham at Villa over the weekend, they were really good, and that'll be a tough game, and you look at some of the games they've got coming.

"It's going to be a tough season for Newcastle. They've got a lot of young players, they've got a young manager in there. The crowd are expecting a lot more."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jaissle opted for a different approach from their defeat against Everton four days earlier, but his tactical changes failed to pay off, with Newcastle not managing a shot on target until the 85th minute.

"Unfortunately we couldn't deliver our style of play across the whole 90 minutes," Jaissle told Sky Sports.

"That's something we are frustrated about. We had a different approach. It looked so good during the week, I have to say the lads were committed to what we were doing and today we can just look back and wonder why we couldn't bring it on the pitch. If you can't deliver when it counts, you don't deserve to win.

"We were not brave enough in possession. Too many long balls. We did not use our double six in possession where we were quite good against Everton a couple days ago. Then it was more of a wide game, back and forth, collecting second balls. That's something that we wanted to avoid to be more dominant.

"It feels at the moment that there's not too much confidence. Not only with the young lads, but also with the more experienced ones. We have to overcome that as a unit. It is expected when you are in transition. Only together we can come out of it.

"After a performance like that, I can understand that [fans booing]. That's a reality and I am responsible for that. We need to work again and again on the things we need to improve. After today, that's a lot."

#989. West Ham sack Nuno Espirito Santo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Hammers, who are close to appointing Scott Parker as Nuno’s replacement, have suffered back-to-back Championship defeats

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

West Ham have sacked manager Nuno Espirito Santo following back-to-back defeats in the Championship and are close to appointing Scott Parker as his replacement.

The Hammers’ promotion campaign has stalled following the home losses to Southampton and West Brom at the London Stadium, with the club sitting eighth after 13 games.

Nuno, who oversaw West Ham’s relegation from the Premier League last season, had been expected to deliver an instant return to the top-flight.

Former West Ham midfielder Parker, who has been out of work since leaving Burnley at the end of last season, is among the candidates to replace Nuno.

A club statement said: “West Ham can confirm that men’s first-team head coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect.

“Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.”

Former West Ham captain Mark Noble, along with Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville, will take temporary charge for Wednesday night’s trip to Cardiff.

The club added that the search for a new head coach is underway, with Nuno’s assistant, Rui Pedro Silva, and goalkeeper coach, Rui Barbosa, also departing.

“West Ham would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future,” the club said.

Nuno, the former Wolves, Tottenham and Nottingham Forest boss, replaced Graham Potter at the London Stadium in September 2025 and had signed a three-year contract.

But the club’s 13-year stay in the top-flight came to an end as they finished 18th and were relegated to the Championship on the final day of the season, with Tottenham staying up instead.

West Ham had opted in May to stick with Nuno, while they retained the services of captain Jarrod Bowen to boost their promotion bid and also secured the Championship record signing of Arne Engels from Celtic for £22m.

The Hammers appeared to be on track for a Premier League return when they thrashed Wrexham 6-0 at the start of September, but that has been followed by just two wins in seven games.

Fans turned on Nuno following the 3-1 defeat to West Brom on Saturday, as many of the 61,125-capacity crowd turned for the exits before full-time following a third home defeat in seven.

Former England international Parker has previously secured promotion from the Championship on three occasions, with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley.

Parker’s former West Ham team-mate Noble could join him in the dugout at the London Stadium following Wednesday’s game at Cardiff.

West Ham currently hold the final spot for the expanded Championship play-offs and are four points below Swansea in the race for automatic promotion.

Under Nuno, West Ham secured a 1-0 win away at promotion contenders Swansea just two weeks ago, before the 3-2 defeat to Southampton and 3-1 loss to West Brom sealed his fate.

#986. West Ham were right to be ruthless with Nuno, but are they right about Scott Parker?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Comment: Some feel it was harsh to sack Nuno now, but truthfully, he could have gone in the summer. The bigger question is whether his reported replacement is the right pick

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

“I am always under pressure, every day,” Nuno Espirito Santo said in the wake of Saturday’s 3-1 loss to West Brom. Not anymore, he’s not.

An optimistic outlook on his removal as West Ham coach is that it offers respite. Respite from that pressure, which has never truly waned in his 13 months in charge. It might seem a ruthless move by the east London club to fire him “so early” into the season, but West Ham were right to be ruthless.

But let’s not forget that the Championship season is already a quarter of the way done, and true ruthlessness would have entailed sacking the Portuguese over the summer, after he failed to stop West Ham from plummeting into the Championship – despite taking over from Graham Potter in late September.

The former Nottingham Forest and Tottenham coach never truly steadied the ship in the Premier League. There was barely even a new-manager bounce to be buoyant about, never a moment when Hammers fans could breathe easily, and even the seas of the second tier (which he navigated so well by winning the league with Wolves in 2017/18) proved too choppy this time around.

That is not to say his West Ham side have been disastrous this season, but with immediate promotion essential from a financial standpoint – and in order to keep the best of this squad together – six wins, four draws, and three losses were never going to instal adequate confidence. Eighth place, one quarter of the way through the season, is too risky a spot.

It is okay to drop points intermittently in such a long, arduous campaign, but the move to sack Nuno was motivated by West Ham’s fear of those points practically spilling out underneath them, like marbles.

It would, of course, have been nice for fans to see a move not motivated by fear; perhaps a change in the summer would have felt harsh, but it would have been proactive, and there is an argument it would have felt encouraging in a different sense.

On the topic of encouragement, West Ham’s free-scoring start to the season was a refreshing sight after recent times at London Stadium, and they remain the highest-scoring team in the division, but their goal difference has already been matched.

And for Nuno, 52, and his players, the issue has not just been conceding too many goals, but also the timing of those errors: they have conceded first in nine out of their 16 games in all competitions. That has signaled a concerning fragility, which has tasked West Ham with fighting back far too often – in a season when many expected them to lead from the front, no less.

Admittedly, there was a degree of naivety to this sentiment. Over the summer, it was all to easy for neutral fans to assume that West Ham would walk the Championship, when supporters of the east London club knew how misguided these claims were. You need look no further than West Ham’s previous outing in the Championship, in 2011/12, when they let a top-two finish slip away before going life and death with Blackpool in the play-off final.

Again, that is far too risky a spot this time around, and cannot be justified when you own the most-expensive squad in the league (at an estimated £282m, with the £18m gap to Wolves proving substantial at this level).

There is surely greater quality at West Ham than any other club in the Championship, and some observers will feel a coach would not need to get too much right to promote the Hammers. In that regard, Nuno was doing too much wrong.

With Scott Parker immediately emerging as the frontrunner to replace him perhaps the conversation can move away from risk. But only in the short-term, you would think.

Parker, a former Hammer, secured promotion with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley in his first season in charge of each club. That record is remarkable. It is simply a shame the stories didn’t end there. Fulham and Burnley were immediately relegated in their following seasons, while Parker left Bournemouth by the end of August after a shocking start to life in the Premier League.

Of course, as a West Ham fan, you might not care to look that far ahead. The priority is purely promotion to the Premier League.

Moreover, a feel-good factor could stem from the nostalgia of Parker’s return. To quote a great modern sketch by Exploding Heads: “He knows the club. He knows the ground... even though it’s different than when he was there.”

In all seriousness, there would be genuine appreciation towards the former midfielder, who won the fan-vote Hammer of the Year award three years in a row. Fans might hope fortunes have been hiding in plain sight.

“Mr West Ham” Mark Noble played alongside the 46-year-old at Upton Park and is now sporting director (he will oversee preparations for Wednesday’s game versus Cardiff). Would Noble and Parker have the chemistry in the office that they had on the pitch? Well, it’s worth noting that they were relegated together in 2011.

Against what you might assume, they would also be unlikely to settle the debate about the “West Ham Way” (chiefly, whether it even exists). While West Ham have scored an unusually high number of goals under Nuno this season, Parker’s M.O. is clean sheets; that would mark a jarring about-turn, stylistically.

But maybe an about-turn is what West Ham need. They are heading in the wrong direction, even if slowly, and slip-ups cannot be allowed to become a full-on skid. West Ham have problems higher up than in the managerial seat, but finding someone to fill it is the only immediate concern.

#985. AI-assisted dying? Doris Dörrie's new film addresses prospect of care robots

While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

Hamburg in the near future: Instead of human drivers, robots deliver parcels. In cafes, robots roll between the tables, serving diners. On the streets, one encounters humanoid robots walking dogs — or the other way around, people taking their robot dogs for a walk.

This is the setting of Doris Dörrie's new film, "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus" ("Mrs. Winkler Leaves the House"). At the core of the plot is an elderly woman who can no longer live on her own after a fall. With her only daughter unable to provide permanent care, the solution seems simple enough: a care robot with a built-in EOL program, or "End of Life" mode. This robot not only assists with everyday life but can also provide assisted dying under certain conditions, namely when the person explicitly wishes to end their life and meets the relevant medical criteria.

Dörrie's film tackles several major social issues with remarkable lightness. These include the challenges facing aging societies such as Germany, Japan and China, the question of dying on one's own terms and a mother-daughter relationship that raises questions of guilt and responsibility. Even though the story is set in Germany, such issues resonate globally.

"I write about what personally moves and interests me," Dörrie told DW.

One of the best-known contemporary German film directors, Dörrie achieved her breakthrough in 1985 with the comedy "Men…" She gained further international recognition with films such as 2008's "Cherry Blossoms" and "Greetings from Fukushima" (2016).

Assisted suicide is one of the most complex ethical questions of our time. Laws vary around the world. Though some countries permit active euthanasia under certain conditions, others prohibit and criminalize all forms of assisted dying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In her film, Dörrie asks what happens when artificial intelligence begins calculating the cost of caring for an elderly person and weighing whether that cost is still "worth" bearing for society.

The underlying idea isn't new, Dörrie said, pointing to the Japanese legend of Narayama, which is also mentioned in the film. According to the legend, the eldest children were responsible for taking their ageing parents to a mountain and leaving them there to die because there was not enough food for everyone. "And that's also the debate we are currently facing to a certain extent: Can we really afford to let older people live longer and longer?"

In Dörrie's film, elderly people are allowed to make their own decisions once they reach a certain state of health — but they can't change their minds afterwards. Yet what does it really mean to make a decision freely? "It's a tricky situation," says Dörrie, because the question is to what extent one is also pressured into making this decision, "not only because it makes more economic sense, but also because one is no longer a burden on one's loved ones — in this case, one's daughter..."

The film often raises these questions indirectly and with plenty of dark humor. At one point, a care adviser presents the EOL feature to Mrs. Winkler as an attractive and, above all, straightforward additional option, making it sound as though there would be nothing more for her to worry about.

Dörrie is not interested in demonizing AI in her film — quite the opposite. In the film, the care robot, which Mrs. Winkler names Pavlovich, helps the elderly woman rediscover some of her zest for life and get out of the house.

"When you travel through Germany, you see small houses everywhere, and statistics show that an elderly person lives alone in every other house," Dörrie said. "If AI can help in these circumstances, why not use it?" She said she sought to explore this ambiguity in her film. Dividing things into black and white would neither be interesting nor, in her view, accurate.

Dörrie and her crew were surprised during filming by how quickly people can develop emotional bonds with robots. She attributes this to the human brain. "We regard anything that moves and speaks as a living being. We can't help it," she explains. And that is precisely what we need to pay attention to when interacting with AI, Dörrie says. "How often are we truly aware that we are talking to a machine rather than a living being? These are things we still have to learn."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As AI develops, it seems that the boundaries between humans and machines are becoming increasingly blurred. That is precisely why we need to talk about it, Doris Dörrie says. In her view, things become problematic "when we can no longer distance ourselves from technology and stop forming our own thoughts."

Human beings need to ask who we are and what truly defines us, Dörrie said. "I believe there is a major difference between robots and us, and that is the ability to play. A robot might be able to initiate a game, she explains, "but play itself is something profoundly human because it has no particular meaning or purpose."

Alongside these philosophical questions about what it means to be human, Dörrie makes a clear call for AI regulation. "At some point, we had to discuss nuclear weapons internationally, too. We've talked about all kinds of issues in the past, and we haven't just talked about them — we've also managed to find solutions," she points out.

"And I believe we need to move very quickly on this, too," Dörrie said.

This article was originally written in German.

Arsenal full-back Riccardo Calafiori could leave the club in a shock move.

Calafiori has been excellent for Arsenal this season – but with the star's contract reaching the two-year mark next summer, the Gunners might have to consider cashing in if they can't extend.

The Gunners won their first fixture at Anfield in 14 years yesterday, with Calafiori a member of the back four that kept yet another clean sheet in the Premier League to go top of the table.

The 24-year-old has arguably been the North Londoners' player of the season thus far, chipping in with goals and assists in attack, while remaining a part of the most impressive back four on the continent.

This has alerted Real Madrid, who are weighing up a move for the defender, as per TEAMtalk.

Los Blancos signed Marc Cucurella over the summer to bolster their options at left-back, but with Calafiori able to play centrally, Bernabeu boss Jose Mourinho is said to value the Arsenal man's versatility, considering him a “dream” signing and Real “enquiring” about a move, after playing the star nine times during his time as Roma manager.

FourFourTwo understands that Real were in the race for the Italian when he eventually left Bologna for North London in 2024, with Arsenal rushing to complete the signing, believing that it was a significant upgrade in that area of the pitch.

But while Calafiori has unlocked a new dimension to manager Mikel Arteta's attack when he's been fit, his contract ticking down – with an expiry in 2029 – may represent an opportunity to sell the star.

FourFourTwo understands that the champions plan to address his extension along with the likes of Martin Odegaard, Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice, though with Calafiori having suffered a number of injuries during his time in English football, Arsenal may have to weigh up whether an attractive bid – and Calafiori's own interest in Real – makes a sale appealing.

Calafiori suffered a potentially career-ending knee injury as a teenager, only to bounce back impressively and rebuild his career via a spell in Switzerland.

Since moving to the Premier League, however, the Rome-born star has suffered eight separate injuries, missing 13 matches in all competitions after Christmas last season, and seeing Piero Hincapie start the Champions League final ahead of him.

Jon Rahm is aware his route back to the PGA Tour is a complicated one and while doubtful he would be once again offered the same deal as Brooks Koepka, he said he would "probably take the penalties".

Rahm quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series "unacceptable".

This occurred when LIV Golf was going through Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the US after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its support at the end of the season, having invested $5bn (£3.7bn) over four years.

Having now left LIV, Rahm is set to return to play on the DP World Tour in 2027, but expressed some uncertainty over his future, admitting he has not yet spoken to the PGA Tour about what a return could look like.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

At the beginning of 2026, Rahm declined the PGA Tour's offer of reinstatement through a specially created Returning Member Program, which was made available to him, Bryson DeChambeau, Cameron Smith and Brooks Koepka.

Koepka was the only player to sign up to the Returning Member Program.

"As of right now, I really don't know what 2027 is going to look like for me," Rahm said, speaking ahead of the DP World Tour's Abu Dhabi Championship, live on Sky Sports from Thursday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I have yet to have a discussion with the PGA Tour to see if there's any path back for next year, so I don't know.

"Until I get clarity on that, my plan would be to spend a year on the DP World Tour. I'm looking forward to it.

"Obviously, Brooks [Koepka] was able to go back through certain circumstances.

"I don't know if the possibility of that would be open for me or not."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

As part of the Returning Member Program, Koepka returned to the PGA Tour under certain conditions, with the American instructed to make a $5m (£3.7m) charitable donation and was excluded from earning equity on the PGA Tour for the next five years.

At present, Rahm will face a one-year suspension from the PGA Tour before he is eligible to win back his card.

"If I have to fulfil a one-year suspension, it's a pretty good position to be in. Worst-case scenario, I get to play in a wonderful tour [the DP World Tour] for a whole year," Rahm added.

"I seriously doubt I will get offered the same deals that Brooks did. But if I got offered exactly the same penalties as him, I probably would do it, yes."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rahm, who tees up at this week's Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship, reflected on his time with LIV Golf positively, but he admitted he did not like the direction the new iteration of the league was heading in, and in the end, it was not much of a "consideration" on whether to stay.

For Rahm, a move away from the team golf element was a big factor.

"Well, I would say I can only reflect on those three years as a positive. It was a wonderful experience; I played a lot of good golf, obviously, individually and as a team. We did great," he added.

"Why did I reject the terms? As much as I liked the project and the idea on, let's say, LIV 1.0, I wasn't thrilled with the changes they were doing to 2.0, and I just wasn't willing to follow that path.

"It wasn't anything special, anything that stood out. I didn't like what they were going with 2.0.

"There were too many unknowns at the time, and there's still quite a few.

"It seemed like it was going a bit away from team golf and some of the things that made LIV. It just became more of a regular tour.

"It wasn't really ever much of a consideration, to be honest."

#982. ‘A perfect scientist, a perfect mum’: researchers mourn two biologists’ deaths in Spanish train crash

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Marta Shahbazi Alonso (left), a rising star in embryology, and Tamara González Costa, who studied heart development, were killed in one of the worst train disasters in Europe in recent times.Credit: MRC LMB/Michael Thornton (L), IMBA Graphics Dept./Hannes Tkadletz (R)

Scientists are mourning the tragic deaths of two developmental biologists who were killed in a train crash in Spain on 28 October.

Marta Shahbazi Alonso, a 41-year-old stem-cell and developmental biologist at the prestigious MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge, UK, and Tamara González Costa, a 31-year-old postdoc at the Institute of Molecular Biotechnology (IMBA) in Vienna, died in a high-speed train collision near the town of Urda in central Spain. The crash, which killed 69 people and injured more than 100 others, is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe’s modern history.

The scientists, who were both originally from Spain, were heading to the 19th meeting of the Spanish Society for Developmental Biology (SEBD) in El Rompido. Shahbazi Alonso, a celebrated embryologist, was travelling to the conference to receive an award recognizing her contributions to the study of human embryo development.

Shahbazi Alonso and González Costa were “two brilliant scientists, with so much talent and so much road ahead, who dedicated their lives to expanding the frontiers of knowledge”, wrote Eva Ortega-Paino, secretary-general for research at Spain’s Ministry of Science and Innovation, on LinkedIn in Spanish. “The grief and emptiness I feel are immeasurable, and nothing comparable to the pain their families suffer today.”

Researchers describe Shahbazi Alonso as an outstanding scientist who made pioneering contributions to extending the time that human embryo models can grow in lab cultures — a notoriously difficult task.

Shahbazi Alonso joined the University of Cambridge in 2014 as a postdoc in the laboratory of leading stem-cell and developmental biologist Magdalena Żernicka-Goetz. “One of the things that I will never forget, and will always stay with me, is her enthusiasm,” says Żernicka-Goetz, who also runs a lab at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. “She loved science for the sake of science.”

In 2016, Shahbazi Alonso and colleagues, working in Żernicka-Goetz’s team, used1 a method to grow human embryos in the lab up to 14 days post-fertilization, up from six days after fertilization in previous efforts. The work allowed scientists to study this crucial stage of human development in unprecedented detail, and provided an alternative to mouse models.

“For the very first time, we can identify features of human embryo life at the time when these many pregnancies fail, and be able to understand what has to happen … for the embryo to survive,” says Żernicka-Goetz.

It was “a real breakthrough”, says Vincent Pasque, a stem cell and developmental biologist at the Catholic University of Leuven in Belgium who knew Shahbazi Alonso.

Shahbazi Alonso's research with Żernicka-Goetz also identified2 ‘molecular checkpoints‘ that coordinate cell development and tissue formation in early embryos.

“Marta was not just an exceptional scientist and a rising star in her field; she was a vibrant, deeply valued member of our institute’s family and part of the future of the LMB,” said Jan Löwe, the LMB’s director, in a press statement on 2 November. “We are devastated by her passing, and our hearts go out to her family, her children and everyone who had the privilege of working alongside her at the LMB and elsewhere.”

Colleagues also speak warmly of Shahbazi Alonso, a mother of two, as someone who skillfully balanced the dual challenges of a demanding scientific career and parenthood. “She was a perfect scientist and a perfect mum,” says friend and collaborator Roser Vento-Tormo, a geneticist at the Wellcome Sanger Institute in Cambridge. Shahbazi Alonso was a passionate scientist, loved by her students and colleagues, and a generous person, she says. “When I was pregnant and I needed to know everything about being a mum, she really shared everything with me” — from food recipes to local schools, she adds.

In 2020, Shahbazi Alonso set up her own research group at the LMB where she continued work on embryo development. “She was a role model for many people around the world, including me,” says Pasque. “The way she combined motherhood and doing science was absolutely stellar.”

“I actually use Marta as a model to my students,” says Żernicka-Goetz, “not just scientific knowledge but also the attitude towards work [and] the focus on science”.

Vento-Tormo says that Shahbazi Alonso’s latest work has made major contributions to understanding aneuploidies — conditions that cause an embryo cell to have extra or missing chromosomes and is associated with pregnancy loss and failure of implantation. Some of this research “will come to light in the following months”.

“She was preparing her tenure file,” says Pasque. “This is a real tragedy for our community.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03564-4

Shahbazi, M. et al. Nature 552, 239–243 (2017).

Carrick appears to have accepted that his tenure at Old Trafford could soon be brought to an abrupt end.

Speaking ahead of Man United’s next game, a Champions League showdown with AS Roma, Carrick was fatalistic in tone when questioned about the mounting speculation surrounding his position.

Rather than offering standard managerial press conference fare of defiance in the face of public scrutiny, the 45-year-old openly acknowledged the reality of his situation.

"I can’t look into the future, I don’t know what’s gonna happen,” Carrick admitted, in quotes via The Athletic. “I am really looking forward to the game tomorrow, you might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had. Whatever happens will happen after that, whatever direction it goes in.”

The mood around the club has turned following a run of just two wins in nine matches across all competitions. A five-game winless streak, an early Carabao Cup exit, and a return of seven points from their opening nine Premier League fixtures has left Man United drastically off the pace.

Recent domestic displays, which include failing to capitalise against 10 men versus Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur, were compounded by a dispiriting Champions League defeat away to Atletico Madrid, after which Lisandro Martinez spoke out against the club hierarchy.

Martinez broke rank to deliver a stinging critique of the club's summer recruitment, reportedly sparking an argument with a teammate on the flight back to Manchester. With a dressing room unravelling and Carrick's gentler approach failing to provoke a response, the popular view is that the club's faith in his faculties to turn things around has plummeted.

To some, his latest quotes indicate a recognition that the writing is on the wall, and with the November international break coming up, that could be the opportune time for the club to sever ties with the former interim head coach.

Old Trafford is likely to have a new first-team manager before long - national outlets have already linked Brighton’s Fabian Hurzeler alongside more experienced coaches Antonio Conte and Unai Emery.

At a club the size of Manchester United, once a manager hums 'que sera, sera', the inevitable is rarely far behind.

#980. Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel dies in hospital after on-pitch collision

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The striker died as a result of injuries sustained in an incident during Tenerife’s second-tier match on Monday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died aged 30 from injuries sustained in an on-pitch collision during a match on Monday.

De Miguel was initially treated on the pitch after he suffered a cardiac arrest following a clash late in added time with Andorra ​goalkeeper ⁠Jesus Owono, before being rushed to hospital. The match was abandoned following the collision.

Tenerife initially reported that he was “stable, despite the severity of his condition” in the intensive care unit of Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz, before reporting that his neurological condition had worsened in the early hours of Tuesday.

The Spanish second division club released a statement saying he had passed away at 8am on Tuesday. It said: “Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, we at CD Tenerife announce the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda.

“There are no words of comfort. There is absolutely nothing that can ease this overwhelming sense of sadness.

“We stand with his devastated family, with his loved ones, and with the entire Tenerife footballing community, who today mourn this cruel turn of events.

The Spanish Football Federation announced the postponed of Tuesday’s Copa del Rey and Copa del Reina matches. “We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones, as well as to Club Deportivo Tenerife and all its fans, whom we accompany in these moments of great sorrow,” it said.

The Spanish Footballers’ Association also expressed its “deep sorrow” at his death, writing: “His loss leaves a huge void among those of us who shared his passion for football, his commitment to the football community, and his work in defense of the rights of fellow professionals.

“The Board of Directors, all the workers of AFE and the footballers’ collective wish to convey our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones, as well as to his teammates at Club Deportivo Tenerife.

“In these moments of immense sadness, we send you all our love, support and solidarity. You will always be part of our family. Rest in peace, comrade.”

A statement from Andorra read: “With broken hearts, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his teammates, friends, and to CD Tenerife. Rest in peace.”

The scoreline was 2-2 when De Miguel was sent through on goal, with keeper Owono rushing out and colliding with him in the chest. Owono, who was shown a straight red card for the challenge, immediately ran to his side as De Miguel appeared motionless, along with other players from both teams and medical staff, before the 30-year-old was taken to hospital.

De Miguel, who made his professional debut in 2015 for Leganes B, signed a three-year contract with Tenerife in 2025 and helped the club earn promotion back to the Segunda Division, scoring 11 goals in 29 games.

Several Spanish teams, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, paid tribute, while Fifpro, the world players’ union, said: “Fifpro is deeply saddened by the passing of CD Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel. Our thoughts are with Jesus’ family, friends, team-mates, everyone at CD Tenerife, and all those affected. Rest in peace, Jesus.”

La Liga president Javier Tebas expressed his shock and said the league would work to support the club and De Miguel’s family, and said he would speak to Tenerife about potentially postponing their next match out of concern for the players’ welfare. Speaking in an interview with Television Canaria, Tebas also raised the possibility of a joint tribute between La Liga and the Segunda Division.

Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin said: “We are heartbroken by the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda. We have searched for words and found only silence. In that silence, our hearts and thoughts are with his family, his team-mates, everyone at Tenerife, and all those who mourn this tragic loss.”

All Uefa matches this week will be preceded with a moment of silence in memory of De Miguel.

This kind of nonsense usually only surfaces around the international break.

An incredible stat, however, has re-emerged concerning Manchester City goalkeeper Ronald Waterreus (remember him?) and his opposite number Nick Colgan (remember him? No?) from around 20 years ago that's sure to blow your mind.

And after digging, it gets even stranger.

Back in 2004/05, only two matches across the entirety of Great Britain in all competitions ended 7-1 – which is not that strange, given that it's an unusual scoreline.

The first came when Man City smashed Barnsley in the League Cup in September, with Waterreus between the sticks for the Citizens and Colgan conceding those seven goals for the Tykes.

The other match that ended with that scoreline, you ask? Well, obviously it was another League Cup game – this time north of the border – between Rangers and Dundee United.

The goalkeepers in that match, you ask? Take a wild guess.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That's right: David James' back-up, Waterreus, had moved to the Gers in search of more game time in January, while Colgan joined United on loan in January 2005.

But the oddness doesn't end there: both matches were club debuts for Waterreus.

The symmetry is startling, especially when you consider that the Dutchman played just a handful of times at City, while Colgan made just two appearances during that stint in Scottish football.

With the fact making its way back onto social media recently, it's probably time to remind everyone of just how much of an incredible coincidence it really is.

So much so, that it featured on a list of extraordinary football facts we published last year…

Lewis Hamilton has called for "serious talks" at Ferrari after his opening lap incident with Charles Leclerc at the Mexico City Grand Prix, while team principal Frederic Vasseur suggested there was not enough "respect" given.

Leclerc attacked Hamilton around the outside going into Turn 4 but outbraked himself and cut the corner to take the lead, while Hamilton lost out to Red Bull's Max Verstappen after briefly going off track.

The stewards gave Leclerc a five-second time penalty which allowed Verstappen to overtake him during the pit stop phase, going on to win the race while Hamilton finished second and Leclerc in fourth.

"Ultimately, it was that, that lost us the win. I think we have to have some serious talks behind the scenes, for sure," said Hamilton.

"But the good thing is the team are working really hard. We've really improved our car. We're on the old engine at the weekend as well, so good result, good points. Shame we didn't get a win, some wins, some losses."

On the team radio during a red flag period for Valtteri Bottas' big crash in his Cadillac, Hamilton stated "we've got big problems" in reference to the Lap 1 incident.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

A frustrated Vasseur says his discussion with the drivers ahead of this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix will be "a matter of respect".

When asked if he could trust his drivers for not putting their individual objectives above the team's, Vasseur said: "This is typically what means respect.

"They are not working for themselves, they are working for a group. They are working for a lot of sponsors. They are working for the 2,000 people of the company.

"The guys, when we had to push for the upgrades, they were working night and day. We have to keep this in mind."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton and Leclerc have found themselves fighting together several times since becoming Ferrari team-mates at the start of 2025.

After being forced wide by Leclerc at the Italian Grand Prix in September, Hamilton accused Ferrari of having "no rules" and demanded "rules of engagement" are required, which he had at Mercedes.

Following their latest incident in Mexico, he said: "I don't know what needs to happen now, how we discuss things when we go back. I'm not quite sure how I want to engage in that.

"Of course, the frustrations are.. I'm happy because Kimi just won the championship, so I'm really torn because, on one side, I'm happy, and on the other side, I'm really p*****.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"We lost valuable points, and we, as a team, worked so hard. We could have easily had a one-two. Really, we had the pace to do so.

"We're going into Turn 4 first and second. If we just hold position, anything can happen in the race, but when your team-mate works against you and then you lose positions like that, it's definitely tough.

"We'll just talk about it offline, and it's not really worth saying too much more. We don't have rules of engagement, and whether or not that will change anything from Charles' side, I don't know. We've just got to figure it out, but something needs to change for sure."

"Charles should have given the place back, but he couldn't because cunning old Max Verstappen got himself in between the two Ferraris as he tried to do back in Madrid earlier this year.

"They're hard-wired racing drivers, it's a curious business we have, where you perform as an individual in a team environment. You're measured as an individual, you're rewarded as an individual, but when the adrenaline is up and the chance of a gap is there, as the great Ayrton Senna used to say: 'If you don't go for a gap, you're no longer a racing driver'.

"Charles has had some frustrations this year, and it doesn't look pretty for the team like when Lando ran into Oscar Piastri in Singapore in the sprint race, it doesn't look pretty for the team and you've let 1,500 people down in your team.

"That's just the car side, without the power unit side. You're only the final link in the chain of the team but you're the one out there that's got to deliver in the heat of the moment. Ferrari will have to manage that somehow.

"They will sit down and we will go to Brazil and they will say 'yes we sat down, we understood it all, we will move forward and it won't happen again' but in reality we know it will."

Consistent team selection and simpler patterns should be the order of the day at Stamford Bridge this season, but Alonso doesn't seem to be offering that yet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The billions spent on young players and the constant churn for accountancy tricks, the erratic form and the bottom-half finishes: Chelsea are engulfed in an identity crisis of their own making and everybody knows Xabi Alonso needs a transitional year to sort this mess out.

What’s needed is stability, order, calm; qualities Chelsea’s owners carelessly abandoned across the first four years of their tech bro, move-fast-and-break-things philosophy. The decision to hire Alonso as ‘manager’ and not ‘head coach’ - and to allow over-30s into the training ground - tells us they have learnt their lesson.

But does Alonso, rocking up in this new and better environment, appreciate the chaos that came before him, that still hums in the background at Stamford Bridge? Judging by the instability, disorder, and erratic tactical setups this season, the answer is no. Alonso is a world-class coach, but he appears to be overthinking his tactics, which is the last thing such a tangled-up squad needs.

In nine Premier League matches, Alonso has used six different combinations in defence and five different combinations of a two-man midfield. As we have highlighted before, he made the strange decision to trial a Henderson-Barco pivot in the defeat at Brentford, and then he got found out by an even stranger strikerless 4-4-2 in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham.

On Saturday, the tactical overthinking was a little harder to spot, but, again, complexity was unnecessarily introduced to a fixture against a Manchester United team waiting to be beaten. Chelsea were a shambles in the first half thanks to a strange use of Cole Palmer that scrambled brains in the middle of the park. When Alonso corrected his error with a far more normal 4-2-3-1 in the second half, Chelsea strode to victory.

In that chaotic end-to-end first half, Chelsea consistently lost possession in the middle of the park (leading to quick United transitions, then quick Chelsea counters back the other way, hence the carnage) because Palmer’s position meant the passing lanes weren’t open. Chelsea, lacking depth (or ‘verticality’), could not pass forward in an orderly fashion and therefore could not maintain a solid shape:

In the second half, Alonso normalised things by playing Palmer higher and suddenly Manchester United couldn’t cope with the passes through the lines.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Even the crucial opener was indirectly affected by this, with Manchester United players seemingly distracted away from Morgan Rogers by Palmer’s lurking presence.

There is a clear lesson here for Alonso: his players – young, new to the club, recovering from the tornado that was 2025/26 – need a firm hand on the tiller; consistent team selection, simple patterns, and the opportunity to discover what it means to play for a normal club.

In other words, these players have spent enough time charging around in circles. They need to be taught how to walk before they can run.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.
