#954. Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?

Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

#952. Which footballers have scored in the same minute as their surname? | The Knowledge

Plus: the longest home droughts, pre-Christmas goal centuries and the first official club websites

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“Justin Seven-Seven came on in the 75th minute and then scored in the 77th minute for West Brom Under-21s against Sutton United in the National League Cup. You have probably already guessed my question, but has anyone else ever scored in the same minute as their name?” wonders Peter Skilton.

Readers of a certain age may recall Didier Six, the mercurial French winger who had a brief spell at Aston Villa in 1984-85. A number of you mentioned some or all of the following sixth-minute goals, which includes two in consecutive seasons against Bordeaux:

Valenciennes 2-1 Nancy (agg: 2-3) Coupe de France quarter-final, 1975-76

Valenciennes 3-2 Bordeaux Ligue 1, 1976-77

VfB Stuttgart 5-1 Karlsruher Bundesliga, 1981-82

We’d imagine Alphonse Six, who won nine caps for Belgium and scored goals galore at club level before he died at 24 years old during the first world war, managed at least one in the sixth minute, but goal times for club football in the 1910s are not easy to come by. Pete Tomlin also offers “Austrian striker Martin Six, who also scored a goal in the sixth minute of a match. He was playing for SV Allerheiligen against DSV Leoben in the Regional League Central on the 1 April 2011.”

“Scottish lower league mainstay Armand Oné scored for Stranraer in the first minute of a League Two game against East Stirlingshire in 2010-11,” writes Richard Wilson, and yes we do believe it. “At the time of writing, son Ryan – at Sheffield United – hasn’t managed the feat, but he has plenty of time.”

This isn’t just an English-language question, as Filippo Varanini points out. “Some Italian football nerd (not me, unfortunately) dug up a Serie C game from 1998, when Raffaele Quaranta (whose surname means 40) scored for Casarano in the 40th minute.” Pete checks back in to mention that “Swiss midfielder Claude Sixt does not strictly have the same name as the number, but he did score a 60th-minute goal in the Swiss League for Sion v Urania Genève on 28 May 1966. Also, Marculino Ninte scored a 90th-minute goal for CD Mafra v SU 1° Dezembro in the third tier of Portuguese football on 5 October 2025.”

We will leave the final, not entirely serious, word to Mark Johnson. “On 2 August 2003, in a match between Banik Ostrava against Slovan Liberec, Marek Heinz (57 varieties) scored in the 57th minute.”

“Burnley have gone a calendar year without a home league win. What is the longest home drought, in the league or in all competitions?” asks our own Niall McVeigh.

Burnley beat Millwall in the FA Cup in January, but it’s 376 days since their last league win at Turf Moor, a 2-0 victory over Leeds on 18 October 2025. Still, could be worse …

“In the NWSL, Sky Blue FC (now Gotham FC) went without a home win between 26 August 2017 and 8 September 2018, a stretch of 378 days,” writes Dave Mellinger. “The victory came over Orlando Pride in their last game of the 2018 season and was their only win, home or away. Had they failed to win, the streak would have rolled on to the start of the next season in April 2019. Unfortunately for us stats nerds, they shocked the world and won that final match.”

Reggiana made no such mistake in Serie A 30 years ago. “Apologies for going all Football Italia on you again,” writes Daz Pearce, labouring under the misapprehension that stimulating the Proustian rush of Football Italia is an act worthy of apology, “but I was quite amused by Reggiana’s magnificent winless home at run in 1996-97, especially as they managed to nick two victories on the road.” Reggiana won their last home game of 1995-96 and the first of 1997-98, both in Serie B. But they did not win a single match at Stadio Giglio in 1996-97, not even in the cups. Their winlessness lasted from 23 May 1996 to 30 August 1997 – a whopping 465 days.

“By my reckoning, Ross County have already scored 81 goals this season: 38 in 10 league games (including beating poor Queen of the South 8-0 and 7-1), 30 in six Challenge Cup group games, 13 in six League Cup games. They may well have scored a century of goals by the end of October! Surely that cannot be bettered. What is the earliest a team has hit a century of goals in a season?” asks Stephen James.

Before we get to a pre-Christmas century from the distant past, we need a modern reference point. Last season, Vincent Kompany’s Bayern Munich reached 100 goals during a 5-1 win at Leipzig on 17 January. This was the breakdown:

Franz Beckenbauer Supercup 2 goals in 1 game

But the Turnbull Tornadoes – as the Hibernian side of the early-1970s, managed by Eddie Turnbull, were known – can beat that by a month. “In 1972-73, Hibernian reached their century of goals on 16 December after beating Ayr United 8-1,” notes Mark Shipway. “They had 41 league goals by then, in 14 games, and had also scored 12 in the Drybrough Cup (three games), 32 in the League Cup (12 games) and 15 in the European Cup Winners Cup (four games).”

Hibs played more games than Bayern, 33 to 28, but that wasn’t the question so pipe down. Their answer to Harry Kane, Michael Olise and Luis Díaz was Alan Gordon, Jimmy O’Rourke and Arthur Duncan, who scored 98 goals between them across the whole season.

That included six of the goals in a legendary 7-0 win at Hearts on 1 January. Weirdly, Hibs’ season ended in a binary fug. In the last eight games, starting with a Cup Winners’ Cup quarter-final defeat to Hajduk Split, the team scored only twice.

“Who were the first football club to have an official website?” wondered Chris White in 2016. “And how about an unofficial website? I noticed that TWTD, Ipswich Town’s unofficial fan site, has been going since 1995, so surely must be one of the first. Also, who were the first clubs to start using social media platforms?”

“I can help,” yelled Martyn Amos, thrusting his arm in the air. “Ipswich Town were, indeed, the first club to have a website (unofficial or otherwise). In fact, I used to help maintain it. It was set up in 1990 by Phil Clarke, who worked at BT in Martlesham (near Ipswich) when the web was still very much experimental. He then passed it on (1993-1995) to Paul Felton, who was a student at UEA in Norwich (boo, hiss).

“After Paul graduated, he passed it on to me as I was, at the time, a PhD student at Warwick (1995-96). Paul then took it back in 1996 and ran it until 2001, when the club finally woke up to the potential of the web, and got a local company called AWS to run it … There used to be some discussion with Sheffield United fans about our claim to primacy, but I believe that it was decided in our favour.”

As for unofficial websites … “Very likely to be Reading’s Hob Nob Anyone which has been knocking around since November 1994,” reckons Peter Sorrill. “Although the distinction between official and unofficial was moot in the early 90s as most clubs weren’t that tech savvy. Here’s the Evening Post’s report on its 20th anniversary from 2014.” In it, the founder Graham Loader explains that “I did computing and then I found out about the internet and realised you could do email and all that stuff. I didn’t think it would get big but it got quite big quite quickly. People would contact me and say how exciting it was that they could read about Reading in places like Canada and Australia.”

But Alex Lopez-Ortiz thought he could go earlier. “The ‘What’s New, September 1993’ NCSA webpage lists: ‘Information on the Sheffield Wednesday Football Club at Nottingham University [website] is online.’ This is very early in the life of the web. NCSA mosaic, which was what popularised the web, was introduced in January of that year.”

“In their 3-0 win over Milan, Bournemouth scored two penalties in the first half taken by different players against two different goalkeepers. Has this ever happened before? And, excluding shootouts, what is the record for the number of penalties scored by one team in a game by different players?” wonders Matthew Wilkie.

“What is the soonest a manager has been sacked after signing a contract extension?” asks Dave Smythe.

“Who was the first manager to wear a tracksuit while watching his team play?” muses Gordon Smith. “I remember that Sir Alf Ramsey used to wear one for England games so did he wear a tracksuit when he managed Ipswich?”

“Newcastle played Hull at 3pm on Saturday 19 September and will play Fulham at 3pm on 7 November at 3pm. All the previous fixtures haven’t been the traditional time,” begins Mark Reilly. “None of our planned fixtures to 7 January against Manchester United are Saturday 3pm kick-offs. What is the fewest number of Saturday 3pm kick-offs in a Premier League season by a club?”

Arsenal are looking to make January business - and one Hull player could be on the radar

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal have been linked with a breakout star of Hull City's good start to the season.

Well plenty expected the Tigers to be rooted to the bottom of the table following a play-off win at Wembley over the summer, Sergej Jakirovic's men have thus far bucked expectations to find themselves midtable, having lost just twice in their opening nine games.

With Premier League champions Arsenal hosting Hull this weekend, too, North London eyes may well be on one of the stars of the Yorkshire club.

Arsenal are back at the top of the table after a win at Anfield over the weekend saw the Gunners climb to the summit for the first time since winning the league last term – but there have been stutters already this season, as they look to conquer on all fronts once again.

Manager Mikel Arteta is apparently already identifying targets in forward areas, according to The Mirror, with dramatic defeats to the likes of Brighton & Hove Albion and Fleetwood Town in the League Cup highlighting the lack of depth that the Basque boss seemingly has in attack.

One potential option is Mohamed Belloumi, according to a new report from Maghreb Foot, via Sport Witness.

The winger has been a revelation in the top flight this season, leading the scoring charts for his club and making his international debut for Algeria this season, scoring two goals in his first three caps for the Fennecs.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Sport Witness relays that Beloumi “couldn’t refuse an offer” from Arsenal, who are now linked with a move for the star.

The 24-year-old certainly fits the profile of an Arteta attacker with excellent work ethic, while his ability to play on both flanks if necessary makes him a potential option for cover.

Arsenal already have the likes of Bukayo Saka, Noni Madueke and 16-year-old Max Dowman to play on the right wing – but with Madueke able to play on the left, Belloumi could be an option to become Saka's deputy, should Arsenal see him as better on that side.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal have their eye on a number of attackers who could strengthen their side either in January or next summer.

RB Leipzig star Antonio Nusa is one particular left-winger who has been linked with the Gunners in recent weeks.

Belloumi is worth €18 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel to Slavia Prague this week as Champions League action continues this week.

#950. In Indonesia, PhD students blow the whistle on bad supervision

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

PhD students at Indonesian universities say that the quality of supervision in the nation is often poor, and that many supervisors engage in inappropriate behaviour.Credit: epsgalery85/Shutterstock

When Rully Charitas Prahmana went to the United States as a visiting lecturer, the academic culture shock was extreme. “I was surprised to see an academic supervisor go cycling with his PhD students on the weekend,” says Prahmana, a mathematics lecturer at Ahmad Dahlan University in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and a visiting researcher at the Western Michigan University in Kalamazoo.

Prahmana can’t imagine that kind of interaction at home, describing himself as being in the minority for occasionally holding informal discussions with students in a warung, small street-food stalls or restaurants that are common across Indonesia. Many of his colleagues never meet their students in casual settings, he says.

PhD candidate–supervisor relationships in the southeast Asian archipelago nation are often less centred around direct scientific supervision in a laboratory or throughout a research project than in much of the rest of the world’s PhD programmes. Many early-career researchers instead say that they only meet supervisors for brief formal discussions, to sign research proposals, or to sign off on their dissertations. Students at larger and more prestigious institutions sometimes have more direct supervision, but “mostly, what we have is power asymmetry”, says Prahmana.

“I met my supervisors routinely but instead of supervising me, they were gossiping about other lecturers,” says one of 11 PhD students interviewed for this article. Several individuals requested anonymity to protect their careers.

Some described being asked to take on tasks at personal expense. One interviewee, for example, said that she had to pay for access to sampling sites before doing her wet-lab research. “I need to take out 200,000 rupiah [around US$12] every week for a year per sampling site,” says the student. All told, she was spending around $1,700 a year on her sampling work. The average monthly salary in Indonesia is around $200.

“I am sure there are many professors who treat students unfairly,” says an anonymous student in Semarang, Indonesia.

“But we are forced to accept what our supervisors say because we just want to graduate soon,” says another.

Some young academics argue that the problem of bad supervisors stems from poor management of PhD programmes in Indonesia, which aims to increase its population of doctoral graduates from around 75,000 to 125,000 by 2045. Brian Yuliarto, the nation’s minister for higher education, science and technology, says that this ambition will drive economic growth. National statistical data are patchy, with broad censuses every ten years, but Indonesia has an estimated 64 million people between the ages of 16 and 30. Yuliarto describes this group — 22% of the country’s population — as “a demography bonus”, telling Nature that the nation needs “to transform them into highly qualified human resources”.

Today in Indonesia, there are 272 PhD holders per one million people, compared with around 14,000 per million in the United States, for example.

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

To boost this number, the Indonesia Endowment Fund for Education, an agency that manages the country’s $9.1-million fund, has set aside money for another 2,500 PhD scholarships this year, says Yuliarto. Nearly half of these will be for those who want to pursue PhD opportunities overseas; the rest will be reserved for people studying partially or fully in Indonesia.

But only some Indonesian universities are set up to provide enough supervision to double the number of people graduating with high-quality PhDs, argues Berry Juliandi, dean of mathematics and natural sciences at IPB University in Bogor. He says that the new funding isn’t supported by strategic policies and regulations around improving academic supervision for the nation’s universities, which will therefore not be able to deliver a high-quality PhD experience.

Indonesia has 4,303 higher-education institutions. The country’s National Accreditation Agency for Higher Education counts only 226 of those as ‘highly qualified’, a criterion that accounts for the quality of not only the physical infrastructure, but also scientific prestige and experience and the teaching skills of the lecturers at the institutions.

Even at these institutions, conflicts between supervisors and PhD students are rife, says Fikri Yanda, a PhD student at Walailak University in Thai Buri, Thailand, who manages the ‘pembela_mahasiswa_indonesia’ (‘Indonesia student advocates’) Instagram account, which discusses academia in Indonesia.

Rully Charitas Prahmana, who teaches mathematics at Ahmad Dahlan University, in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, says that there is often a power asymmetry between PhD supervisors and students in Indonesia.Credit: Rully Charitas Indra Prahmana

So far this year, Indonesia’s ministry of education has reported 874 cases of inappropriate behaviour, including ethical misconduct, violence, sexual harassment and abuse of power.

This kind of behaviour “hampers our freedom to think freely as academics”, says Andik Wijayanto, a biology PhD student at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta, because scientists aren’t able to challenge the status quo. Many students are afraid to make mistakes, he says. (Wijayanto, who also lectures in biology at the State University of Malang in East Java, says that he doesn’t have any problems with his own supervisors.)

In 2017, Indonesia’s higher-education ministry found that of 5,366 professors in Indonesia, 3,800 had not published peer-reviewed papers in international journals that the government considered reputable. This led to stricter regulations that now require all professors and other university lecturers with master’s and doctoral degrees of all disciplines to publish in high-quality Scopus-indexed journals. But the policy backfired: some academics were snared by predatory journals — organizations that offer to publish papers for a fee, often using aggressive or misleading solicitation practices, while not providing legitimate peer review or adequate editorial assistance. Other researchers manipulated their citation indexes to achieve high performance scores in the government’s evaluation system.

In 2021, the ministry introduced a regulation on scientific integrity that sanctions scientists who engage in data fabrication, plagiarism and forged authorship. This was followed by another regulation signed by Yuliarto this February, which asks institutions to assess ‘scientific integrity’ when evaluating university lecturers’ performance, a determining factor for their career opportunities.

#949. WSL talking points: Kang could have a problem and how long can Slegers hang on?

Arsenal dropped points again despite dominating while Lauren James had to go off in Chelsea’s 6-0 win at Charlton

London City Lionesses may have lost 2-1 to champions Manchester City, but their performances and league position have shown their European aspirations are far from unrealistic. Aided by Arsenal’s poor start, London City are third in the WSL table and were frustrated to end the day with a six-point gap to the top two after dominating in Bromley. “It’s doubly frustrating, because I think the result was not the one we deserve,” said their coach, Eder Maestre. “Manchester City are more mature. They are more used to it. When you have this consistency and you are very used to playing these kinds of games, maybe you have more experience.” Maestre’s team have a three-point lead over fourth-placed Tottenham and if they continue their upwards trajectory and qualify for the Champions League, Uefa will be forced to tackle the possible scenario of two Michelle Kang-owned clubs, London City and OL Lyonnes, qualifying sooner than they perhaps anticipated. Suzanne Wrack

Manchester United’s current predicament could get worse before it gets better, with reports in Germany suggesting that director of recruitment Christopher Vivell is on the verge of joining Bayern Munich.

As the Old Trafford hierarchy wrestles with growing scrutiny, accusations of a lack of leadership and a fractured dressing room, the loss of one of their footballing strategy leads threatens to cause further operational problems.

According to a report from Sport Witness, Vivell is being lined up by Bayern Munich.

The German executive’s potential exit comes at an inopportune time for the Red Devils, who are currently navigating issues on and off the pitch.

Vivell’s tenure in Manchester has been relatively brief but significant. Initially brought in ahead of the 2024/25 season on a short-term, interim basis, his influence within the new INEOS-led regime quickly grew.

By February 2025, Man United had seen enough to appoint him as their full-time director of recruitment, giving him responsibility to oversee the club’s global talent identification and squad-building.

However, Vivell's long-term vision now appears to have been compromised by the current chaos and lack of results at Old Trafford.

Man United are enduring a disastrous spell at present with one win from their opening nine Premier League games this season, leaving them languishing at the wrong end of the table.

At the centre of it all is first-team boss Michael Carrick, whose own future hangs in the balance. The manager is essentially operating under a stay of execution with many expecting the axe to swing before long.

It is the belief of some Man United outsiders that a lack of unified leadership in key positions has negatively impacted the club's decision-making processes.

Reports indicate that Vivell and director of football Jason Wilcox do not see eye-to-eye over the succession plan should Carrick be formally dismissed. While the club has reportedly shortlisted high-profile candidates, including Julian Nagelsmann, Fabian Hurzeler, and Antonio Conte, the inability of the football leadership team to align on a common direction has only exacerbated the crisis.

If Vivell were to accept Bayern Munich’s overtures, it would leave a void in Man United's recruitment department just as the club faces the prospect of yet another mid-season managerial change. Having an established working relationship with Bayern sporting director Christoph Freund, Vivell is, on paper at least, a natural fit for the German giants.

With the January transfer window fast approaching and Carrick’s future unclear, Manchester United can ill afford to lose their recruitment chief.

#945. Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson

Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team

For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes.

This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League?

Brentford began the weekend in third and with, perhaps, a slight sense of frustration that they had drawn four games. Again, they will feel they might have done rather better on Saturday; they were leading Liverpool 1-0 when Yehor Yarmolyuk foolishly flicked his head towards Jérémy Jacquet and was sent off just before half-time. The result was a 2-1 defeat and a sense of an opportunity missed. Bournemouth have not had the easiest start under Marco Rose, but Sunday’s 2-0 win over Sunderland perhaps hints at a brighter future.

Which left Brighton to carry the charge of the B clubs, which they did in emphatic style, ending a run of four derbies without success with a crushing 5-0 win. Crystal Palace had been extremely fortunate to survive a first-half battering from Nottingham Forest last week. They were thoroughly outplayed in the early stages again, and this time found themselves 3-0 down inside 10 minutes. Perhaps the opening goal, a cross headed into his own net by Jaydee Canvot, was fortunate, but it was an error induced by the intensity of Brighton’s start. The second goal, a perfectly weighted drive from just inside the Palace half from Diego Gómez, spoke of a side playing with immense confidence. Already this season, 11 different players have scored for Brighton in the league. They have become the image of a side without stars, the whole far greater than the individuals who comprise it.

The difference from February, when Brighton last played Palace, is stark. They lost that game 1-0, meaning they had won just one of their previous 12 Premier League games. Generalised grumbling had begun to curdle into calls for Fabian Hürzeler to be sacked. When they lost Carlos Baleba, Jan Paul van Hecke, Danny Welbeck and James Milner over the summer, there were reasons to wonder whether they could keep going with the process of continuous renewal.

There were the usual assorted signings, the usual mix of Premier League experience and exotic unknowns. The 19-year-old centre-back Luka Vušković, who spent last season on loan at Hamburg from Tottenham, already looks at home (and who really thought, when Spurs and Brighton effectively swapped centre-backs, with Van Hecke moving to London, that Brighton would not end up with the better of the deal?). The 21-year-old Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés, who arrived from Stuttgart, sparkled from the bench against Arsenal and has excelled in the two games since.

But the stand-out performer this season has been a far more familiar name: Pascal Gross, who returned in January after a season and a half at Borussia Dortmund. No player in the Premier League has registered more than his four assists this season. Nobody has run further. He has three goals. He averages a league-high 3.0 key passes a game. To bring back a player who is now 35 has been a masterstroke.

The victory over Arsenal before the international break suggested a team capable not merely of accumulating points against the league’s lesser lights, or even of challenging the elite, but of overwhelming them. Arsenal were suffocated by the Brighton press and, while a couple of low-xG long-range finishes in the first half helped, the fact is that Brighton dominated the match to a remarkable extent.

The question is whether they can keep it going. Just as their transfer policy is now an accepted feature of the Premier League, so too is Brighton’s mid-season slump. They haven’t won a game in December since 2023. Is this squad strong enough to sustain the challenge? Europe seems not to be unsettling Brighton as it did on their first foray, or as it appears to be draining Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Sunderland – which may be a reflection on the relative quality of the Conference League.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

They are doing this without Kaoru Mitoma, Yankuba Minteh and Mats Wieffer, all of whom should be back at some point over the next month. That suggests the depth of this Brighton squad. It’s always a major step for a club unfamiliar with the Champions League to haul themselves into the top five. At times it often feels a mental barrier as much as anything.

But if any of those B clubs are ever going to break into the Champions League, they may never have a better opportunity than Brighton do this season.

#944. The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion

Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

#942. The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s tragic arc | Jonathan Wilson

There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment

And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.

But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically?

It’s worth remembering where all this began. The United story has taken on the aspect of a classical tragedy and, like all good tragedies, it begins with a small, seemingly unconnected moment, amplified by pride, that ends up bringing the whole edifice crashing down.

In 1999, Mull of Kintyre, a horse owned by the Irish millionaire John Magnier, won the Gimcrack Stakes at York. Traditionally, the winning owner would give a speech at the Gimcrack Dinner, but Magnier was a shy man who hated public speaking so he asked his friend, the United manager Alex Ferguson, to give the speech on his behalf. The racing establishment, though, refused: it had to be the owner. To spite them, Magnier named Ferguson as the owner of another horse, Juniper. The following year, Juniper was narrowly beaten in the Gimcrack Stakes. Magnier, though, was determined. So the year after that, he made Ferguson the owner of Rock of Gibraltar, which had won its first three races. Rock of Gibraltar won the Gimcrack easily and Magnier, waving a metaphorical two fingers at the racing authorities, watched Ferguson give the speech.

Magnier was largely making mischief, but he was also happy to do a favor for a friend, to give Ferguson a better experience of racing, and he benefited from the association of the horse with such a famous name. In addition, Ferguson did not get on well with the United chairman, Martin Edwards, and had a sense that football clubs were becoming good investments. Accordingly Magnier and his associate JP McManus bought shares in United. (The full story is explored by the journalist David Walsh here).

It turned out, though, that Rock of Gibraltar was a much better horse than anybody had realized, winning seven Group One races in a row. The stud fees would be worth tens of millions of pounds. Ferguson believed the verbal deal was that he could choose 50% of the prize money won by Rock of Gibraltar (about £800,000) or 50% of the stud fees, which ended up being worth tens of millions. He went for the latter. Magnier’s recollection was rather different: 5% of the prize money or one stud nomination a year.

Ferguson sued and, with his name on the ownership documents, probably would have won had it gone to trial. But then rumors started to spread about some of Ferguson’s financial dealings at United. Paid actors at United’s annual general meeting raised awkward points, then Magnier and McManus sent a list of 99 questions to the United board, which mysteriously found their way into the Daily Mail. United were highly embarrassed. Fans began to demonstrate against Magnier and McManus at race meetings. A settlement was reached, with Ferguson paid £2.5m to drop the action. But the damage was done.

Magnier and McManus had decided to sell their shares in United, and another shareholder was ready and waiting: Malcolm Glazer. Ferguson backed Glazer, who launched his leveraged buyout. Magnier and McManus sold up in 2005 for £260m, a profit of a little under £100m. Had they waited for Ratcliffe, who bought a similar stake in 2024, they would have received roughly £1bn more than that. For Ferguson, a threat had been dealt with.

The problem was that Glazer and his family would prove some of the worst club owners in English history. For 20 years, United have been addled by debt and have made consistently terrible footballing decisions. Ferguson’s team was good enough, and his personality big enough, that United won five league titles and a Champions League after the takeover, but once his genius had gone, there was nothing left.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

A mismatched squad built up over seven flawed managerial appointments and a multiplicity of conflicting approaches will not readily be sorted out. Carrick is the latest victim of a crisis 21 years in the making. For the want of a horse a club was lost.

#941. Man Utd beware! Malen is a man transformed at Roma

Donyell Malen has been on fire in front of goal for Roma since signing from Aston Villa and that makes him the last man Manchester United want to face in the Champions League. Adam Bate examines the transformation of the Netherlands international in Italy

Football Features Writer @ghostgoal

The top scorer in Europe’s major leagues in 2026 is not Harry Kane or Kylian Mbappe, not Erling Haaland or Lamine Yamal. That honour belongs to Donyell Malen. A revelation at Roma, he makes his return to England against Manchester United on Tuesday night.

Malen was a popular figure at Aston Villa but even his biggest admirers might not have anticipated all this. Fourteen goals in 18 Serie A games on loan last season certainly suggested that Roma could get the best from him but Malen has gone to another level.

He began with a hat-trick against Fiorentina and now has eight goals in eight Serie A games. There was a suspension for a red card in there too but it hardly stopped him. He goes to Old Trafford on the back of goals against Cagliari and Udinese in the past week.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

In 2026, Malen has scored 18 goals from open play, two more than nearest rival Lamine Yamal and four more than anyone else in the big leagues. Just an Italian thing? Not quite. In the Champions League, Malen bagged a brace against Real Madrid last month.

The obvious question is how and why this is happening. Now 27, Malen felt like a known quantity in European football. It is over a decade ago that he was a youngster at Arsenal. Speaking to him last year about those early days, he explained: "I was this skinny [kid]."

He was honest enough to admit that it all came too soon for him. "I was only 16 when I trained with the first team. Maybe I was not really 100 per cent ready. Looking back, I learnt a lot in those two and a half years there. But I made my steps in a different way."

At PSV, he was prolific. But his big move to Borussia Dortmund saw him deliver only sporadically. Malen certainly had his moments but nothing sustained like this and he was perhaps a victim of his ability to play in various different positions across the front line.

Speaking to Unai Emery at the time of his arrival at Villa, that versatility was part of the appeal. "We are practising with him in different positions, attacking third, sometimes right side, which is a little bit of a priority, but as well as a No 10 and as a striker."

Malen offered the usual spiel about being relaxed about his role. "I have played all the positions by now at this stage, so for me it does not really matter." But there was one line when talking to him that betrayed his true feelings. "I just want to be close to the goal."

Emery knew this, of course. "He likes to be close in the opponent's goal and he likes to score goals." But Villa had Ollie Watkins up front. It has taken Gian Piero Gasperini to bring out the best in Malen over an extended period. He has done so by unleashing him up top.

"He wanted to be a centre-forward, and I always thought that is where he was stronger too because he is deadly near the penalty area." The experienced Roma coach did add an important caveat. "Admittedly, I did not expect his numbers to be so astonishing."

There have been the familiar power finishes but two of his goals past David de Gea in the Fiorentina game were with his left foot. At Lecce, there was a delightful dink. There have been poached efforts and examples of him showcasing his prodigious speed from deep.

It is easy to recognise it now but Gasperini's style of play seems ideally suited to a player with Malen's skill-set. The man-to-man approach emphasises his quality in one-on-one situations, where his pace and dribbling ability makes him a match for anyone.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Once in behind the defence, which happens often with Gasperini's vertical game, there is no catching him either. "Running in behind, trying to create space for midfielders. I think that is my strength." No one in Serie A has had more touches in the opposition box.

Can Manchester United stop him? The recent record of their sluggish and sloppy defence suggests that Malen could be their worst nightmare. He makes the trip to Old Trafford as a different proposition to the player last seen on these shores in January.

With his coach likening him to the late great Gianluca Vialli because of his "similar ability to shake off his marker and get in behind" defences, this is a different Donyell Malen. One boasting a scoring record that shows he is the deadliest striker in Europe right now.

The Left Party is hoping to have Elif Eralp lead the state government.

The coalition talks are set to open after weeks of tense negotiations and a dispute over alleged antisemitism within the ranks of the Left Party.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang unveiled a new artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation at a glitzy investment summit in Berlin on Monday evening.

"Germany is open for business," said Merz at the Invest in Germany event, adding that the combination of German engineering and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy in the long term.

"Germany is open for investment and Germany is ready to grow at a faster pace," the chancellor continued, before joking: "If I were Jensen Huang, I would put on my leather jacket, take a flight to Berlin, meet the German Chancellor, and tell him, 'I'm ready to invest.'"

The partnership with Nvidia is intended to speed up the digital transformation of German industry and secure the country's technological sovereignty.

According to the company, Nvidia invested nearly $1 billion in Germany last year and holds stakes in numerous start-ups and established companies.

But Europe's largest economy has nevertheless struggled to attract foreign investment after years of weak growth, with high energy prices and labor costs continuing to deter businesses.

German officials were hoping that Monday's summit, which was attended by more than 200 domestic and international investment executives, would showcase Germany as an attractive investment destination, highlighting its sound public finances, status as the only G7 country with a triple-A credit rating, its universities, skilled workforce and tariff-free trade within the EU single market.

Further behind-closed-door talks are set to take place on Tuesday.

Do you remember those arrests in Germany last week, connected to an arson attempt at a Starlink control center in Poland?

The government in Warsaw called it a hybrid attack and accused Russia of recruiting organized crime elements for the alleged crime.

It's much too early to say for sure, but Bulgaria has now issued a pair of European arrest warrants against German citizens in a case that seems rather reminiscent in several regards.

The two 19-year-olds are accused of driving in from Serbia claiming to be tourists, setting fire to a series of antennae south of Sofia, and leaving the country again within a matter of hours.

Hermann Höllenreiner, a Sinti German raised in Bavaria who survived the Nazis' Auschwitz concentration camp as a child, has died aged 92.

Munich's Hanser Verlag publisher and the International Auschwitz Committee said that he had passed away last Friday, October 16, in Mettenheim in Bavaria, surrounded by his family.

Höllenreiner, known as "Mano" to his large Bavarian Sinti family, spent time at the Auschwitz-Birkenau, Ravensbrück and Sachsenhausen camps as a child.

"Only later in his life did he start to tell his story and became a major witness of the era, who hauntingly reported on the horrors of Auschwitz, the perpetrators and the victims, and above all of the still-persistnent discrimination of Sinti and Roma in Europe," Christioph Heubner, executive vice president of the International Auschwitz Committee, said.

"Mano Höllenreiner's biography and tales of suffering were enough for more than one life. What he saw with his own eyes as a child in Auschwitz and what was done to him — for many decades he didn't know how to speak out about it," Heubner said, thanking Höllenreiner for his "courage and humanity" in ultimately telling his story.

Höllenriener managed to flee one of the so-called "death marches" fleeing extermination camps in as Allied armies approached.

Author Anja Tuckermann told his story in a book whose title roughly translates as: "Mano. The boy who didn't know where he was."

He was initially found on a roadside and rescued by liberated French prisoners, who took him home with them. In 1946, he was reunited with surviving relatives in Germany.

Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.

The two, aged 20 and 32, handed themselves in to the police on Sunday evening, following the incident. The broken fence was first discovered by airport staff late on Saturday.

Police said the 20-year-old had been at the wheel despite not having a valid license.

An investigation was opened into the learner driver for fleeing the scene after breaking through the fence.

The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.

The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.

German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.

Germany's Rheinmetall defense group on Monday announced that it had acquired Romania's Mangalia shipyard at auction in partnership with Swiss shipping giant MSC.

Rheinmetall said it had paid approximately €138 million ($154 million) for the facility.   Acquisition is expected to be finalized within a few weeks.   Rheinmetall and MSC plan to develop the Black Sea shipyard near Constanța into a dual-use site for civilian and military shipbuilding for both domestic and international markets.

Rheinmetall says its Naval Systems division will use the facility to build four vessels commissioned by the Romanian government, including two 96-meter (305 foot) offshore patrol vessels and two 43-meter diving support vessels.   The company also intends to modernize the shipyard's infrastructure and expand its capacity.

"In doing so," said the company, ​"Rheinmetall ⁠is creating a scalable foundation for future ⁠projects in ​southeastern Europe and strengthens its position in a strategically important market."

The Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran.

"We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X.

"We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote.

A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG).

In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of  Schuster and Beck.

The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force.

The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations.

German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.

Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.

But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.

At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.

It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.

Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.

"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.

"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."

A German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday.

The 32-year-old woman, who was an experienced mountaineer, fell more than 50 meters (164 feet) to her death while on the Cengia dei Camosci, a difficult route on the 2,323-meter Grande Nabois mountain near the Slovenian border.

The rescue service said the accident was caused when a climbing hold gave way under the woman, who was accompanied by an Austrian fellow climber at the time.

Investigations are underway to clarify the exact circumstances of her death.

Carmaker Volkswagen intends to freeze the salaries of some 660,000 employees worldwide until 2030 as the company, along with the entire car industry, faces a range of challenges that have impacted its profits.

Trade union IG Metall confirmed earlier media reports of the plans, citing information given to employees by the works council.

The works council described the plans as unrealistic and said there would be considerable resistance to them.

If the company does implement them, employees could lose an estimated 10% of their purchasing power by the end of the decade.

The news comes after VW decided in September to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years in addition to the reduction of 50,000 positions that had already been agreed.

Four plants in Germany are also at risk of being closed between 2031 and 2034.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.

According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.

Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.

"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.

Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.

A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

The DW newsroom in Bonn bids guten Tag to all its faithful readers at the start of a new week!

Today, we will be looking at a conference in Berlin that will seek to attract private investment in Germany to help make the country fit for the future, with the field of artificial intelligence a key focus.

New statistics are also to be released on Monday on women in leadership and government positions in Germany and the EU in 2025.

And the Leipzig/Halle airport has resumed normal operations after a security incident involving a breached fence triggered a large-scale police operation.

This occurred just weeks after an explosives-laden drone that German officials believe was intended to carry out an attack on behalf of Russia was found at the airport.

Read on for more on these and other stories connected with all things German.

#939. Rodman rule has been revised but the fight to keep stars in the NWSL goes on | Moving the Goalposts

Gone are the eight criteria to be a High Impact Player so clubs can spend their money on whomever they want – and the solution makes sense

When Washington plays Chicago this Sunday in DC, “Rowdy Audi” will probably be full. It will also be full when the post-season starts, should they lock up their top-four position with a positive result on Decision Day. Equipped with an accessible stadium in a big city, a proud fanbase and a formidable roster rife with players qualifying for the High Impact Player (HIP) rule’s initial criteria (including Trinity Rodman, who gave the rule its moniker), the Spirit hold sway in the attendance charts.

But starting next season, everyone on the Spirit will qualify for the “Rodman Rule”. So will every player in NWSL. Announced Friday, NWSL settled a grievance with the league’s Players Association, who argued that the initial criteria violated federal labor law.

Admittedly, when the new policy arrived on the scene last winter, it appeared half-baked, a somewhat frantic attempt to keep Rodman from floating across the Atlantic and doing something terrible, like playing for Michele Kang’s London City Lionesses instead of Michele Kang’s Washington Spirit.

A rule was born to prevent that. It allocated added funds beyond the salary cap for players who met league-set criteria that clearly prioritized international name recognition in a global market. Qualifying players needed to meet one of eight categories including SportsPro Media’s top 150 Most Marketable Athletes (only Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmatí placed in 2026, though 16 female football players did in 2025, including three in the NWSL at the time – Trinity Rodman, Sophia Wilson and Marta, in that order). It also included ESPN’s Top 50, the Guardian’s top 100, top minutes on the US national team, the Ballon d’Or’s 30-player list, or NWSL’s MVP and Best XI awards.

Some measure of umbrage followed, as invested onlookers argued for a simpler solution: just raise the salary cap. And perhaps they should, but keeping an American-style sports league competitive in a global football landscape is less straightforward. The looming spectre of Europe’s super-teams, who have attracted key members of the USWNT starting XI, is ever present, waiting to take Croix Bethune away for the right amount of money. No doubt, the NWSL’s appeal is evident in its expansion and growth, in the success of its spine of stateside stalwarts, in its rapidly expanding dedicated facilities, and in the international talents such as Esme Morgan or Ann-Katrin Berger that choose to sharpen their skills in the US.

However, the domestic sporting culture of the NWSL is somewhat at odds, in some ways a disadvantage, when it comes to maintaining its margins, with a stand-alone team structure in a parity-driven league, while competing for international glory with teams such as Chelsea, Lyon or Barcelona, who spend three times or more the amount that some NWSL teams do. While competing for status as the world’s go-to destination, for players and fans, glory hunting and name recognition do matter.

Just look at the Ballon d’Or: Barcelona’s women took all but one of the awards available to them, though Alexia Putellas, who collected her third main prize, now plays in London. That Putellas deserves her trophy is not in dispute, though the inequitable factors contributing to international accolades were manifest. Putellas starred for two super-teams: Barcelona and Spain. Ewa Pajor, Barcelona’s Polish striker, fell just short, perhaps edged out by only having one super-team to play for.

Subtly, it seemed, the original criteria for the HIP rule flirted with the idea of fostering a super-team in the US. Prior to the update, there was no cap on the number of players who could access the extra million if the salary cap was already met. For a team such as Kang’s in Washington, the door felt open, possibly, to building a team even more ready to contend with the heavy spenders in Europe (including those also funded by Kang), and the international accolades that go with it. If a NWSL player lifted the NWSL trophy, helped win January’s inaugural Club World Cup, then performed well at the World Cup, could a second NWSL (active) player win the Ballon d’Or?

The structure of the HIP rule remains in place. Teams that have met 2027’s salary cap of $4.4m (£3.3m) in 2027 can spend an additional $1.257m (as reported by ESPN) on a player. The post-grievance difference is that teams can spend that additional sum on any player. Gone are the stipulations mandating adherence to that eight-criteria list of global recognition.

The change is a win for players that did not meet it, which includes elite players who fell short in previous seasons (such as Ashley Sanchez) or star players with long-lasting or recurring injuries (Catarina Macario). It gives the NWSL’s individual teams the autonomy to decide which players are worthy, based on whatever criteria they see fit. And, with a cap on the number of players that can access it, it gives cash-strapped teams the theoretical ability to rein in teams with already-stacked rosters.

But the spirit of NWSL’s original criteria has more merit than many suggest. The NWSL is responsible for securing overhead issues such as an improved media rights deal, marketing marquee names to broadcasters, ensuring the league is seen as the go-to destination before a World Cup and performing well in global cup competitions such as the Concacaf W Champions Cup (Mexico’s Club América prevailed in the most recent final) or the upcoming Club World Cup. With that in mind – plus the ever-pressing desire to keep USWNT players in the US – the original HIP criteria had its eye on awarding stardom as it’s seen in the global market.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Stardom is imprecise. It’s hard to measure, but impossible to miss. Rodman did not make the Ballon d’Or shortlist and is not leading the Golden Boot race. But Rodman and her closest national team peers (including “Triple Espresso” compadres Mallory Swanson and Wilson) are the presumed stars of the NWSL. Rodman, alongside Wilson (who clocked the Michael Jordan “shrug” celebration after scoring in the 2022 Championship final) have not just the skill but the personality flourishes reminiscent of Alex Morgan sipping the tea in Lyon.

The NWSL has yet to replicate the Morgan effect (think default attendance records and adoring away fans), but requiring that teams reward players with a certain je ne sais quoi in their international football fame was baked into the league’s original attempt at the HIP criteria.

If you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please email moving.goalposts@theguardian.com.

This is an extract from our free email about women’s football, Moving the Goalposts. To get the full edition, visit this page and follow the instructions. Moving the Goalposts is delivered to your inboxes every Tuesday and Thursday.
