#869. Are Manchester United really at risk of a relegation scrap?

Chelsea beat 10-man Man Utd to pile more pressure on Michael Carrick

"We've got to keep moving forward and winning games, simple as that," said Michael Carrick in that considered way of his, after their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea on Saturday.

Carrick did get relegated once, with West Ham at the start of his playing career.

The Hammers were supposed to be too good to go down in 2002-03. Aside from Carrick, they had England goalkeeper David James in their squad. Joe Cole, Jermain Defoe and Trevor Sinclair all played more than 40 games in all competitions.

But down they went, finishing third bottom with 42 points. It remains the highest tally any side has been relegated with across a 38-game Premier League campaign.

To put that into context, Manchester United's current tally of seven points from nine games would not even get them 30 points if it was continued for the full season.

So, are United really destined for a relegation scrap?

Chelsea v Manchester United - Michael Carrick post-match

You would have to be touching 60 to have any recollection of the last time United were relegated.

Legend has it that old boy Denis Law sent them down with an impudent back heel he didn't celebrate when he was at Manchester City. The reality is United were already doomed under then-boss Tommy Docherty.

United have not been in the relegation zone after nine games or more since November 1986, when they collected a single point in Sir Alex Ferguson's first two games in charge following Ron Atkinson's dismissal.

Their lowest position after at least nine games of a season since then was 17th in 1989-90. They are back there again right now, mainly thanks to the failings of others in results elsewhere on Saturday.

It is now nine games in all competitions since Carrick's side won, their worst run since 1988-89. Their single Premier League win of the season was when they came from behind to beat Ipswich at home in August.

Of course, United's supporters have very recent experience of seeing their team in the lower reaches of the table. They were 16th under Ruben Amorim after 37 games of the 2024-25 season. The caveat is they were 14 points clear of third-bottom Leicester and at no point in that tortuous campaign were they in danger of relegation.

One club that has been at real risk in recent years is Tottenham, who were third bottom and two points behind West Ham with four games of last season remaining.

So, it could happen, even if it remains unlikely a club that should post revenues in excess of Â£700m for the current campaign will finish in the bottom three.

"You can look at it like that, or you can look at how far you can move up the league quite quickly if you win football matches," was Carrick's response when asked if his players are equipped for the "mentality shift" required to deal with the present situation. "That's the way it's got to be approached."

Martinez's 'inexplicable' 83 seconds cost Man Utd and Carrick

Rogers shines, 3/10 for sent-off Martinez - player ratings for Chelsea v Man Utd

Chelsea beat 10-man Man Utd to heap further pressure on Carrick

Has Martinez become a liability for Man Utd?

Yet, as Carrick said, in order to save themselves, United need to win matches.

Their next game is against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on 8 November. Among the seven matches they have after that are trips to Liverpool, Newcastle and Arsenal.

As yet, there is no word about Carrick's future, although before Saturday's loss, the expectation was he would be in charge for Tuesday's Champions League encounter with Roma.

But these are uncharted waters and no-one can be absolutely sure what happens next. It is clear that many players need to improve their performance levels.

United will be without one of those players, Lisandro Martinez, who will miss the Villa game due to suspension after his red card at Chelsea, which was branded "inexplicable" by former World Cup final official Darren Cann on BBC Sport.

Martinez's longer-term future with the club is uncertain, but clearly he could not leave until January at the earliest.

His contract expires in the summer, and the Argentine's patchy injury record had already raised questions over whether it was worth triggering the clause that would commit United to another season.

United are winless in their last nine games in all competitions - they last had a longer run in September 1984 (10 games)

After just nine games, it is a bit early to dig into the actual consequences of relegation for United, but the numbers might offer pause for thought.

In May, respected football finance blogger Paul Quinn, known as The Esk, calculated that Tottenham's "absolute revenue loss", external would be between Â£197m-Â£235m if they did go down.

As one of the league's highest recipients of TV income, United would not remotely be covered by the parachute payments available to relegated clubs.

It seems unlikely that many, if any, of their squad would have relegation clauses, and while United have huge commercial income, it is not known to what extent that would be affected by clauses triggered by relegation.

United also have Â£1.15bn worth of debt, made up of bonds that were renegotiated in June at a higher interest rate, a revolving credit facility and outstanding transfer fee payments.

The club are also about to launch a fan consultation before coming up with final plans for a new stadium, which are due to be submitted either in late 2027 or early 2028.

United fans once again chanted their opposition to a new stadium at Stamford Bridge during the Chelsea defeat.

It is a complicated picture, and even though it seems highly unlikely that the doomsday scenario will become reality, the mere fact that United are in the position they are underlines just how poor their form has been.

#863. SZA's Vans Collab Has These Viral Styles Still in Stock

The VANSZA collaboration offers unisex utilitarian footwear, apparel and accessories curated by the R&B artist. Inspired by the Gold Coast's natural beauty, shop the celeb drop worth bugging out over.

SZA has joined forces with storied skate brand Vans as its first-ever artistic director, and their first VANSZA collection is officially here.

The capsule collection marries the artist’s earthy personal style with Vans’ love for the great outdoors, bringing together limited-edition clothing, accessories, and two pairs of reimagined Vans classic sneakers that are surprisingly still in stock, for now: the Knu Skool Mule and the Authentic Kickdown, now SZA-fied.

The workwear-inspired capsule features nature-loving details—think camo prints, motifs of fish and insects—that fit right into SZA’s world, as well as Vans heritage. Standout ready-to-wear pieces include a crewneck fleece sweatshirt and sweatpants set innovatively printed to look like a worn-in work jacket and trouser—all the cozyness of a hoodie, but none of the labor.

This black suede mule reimagines the classic Knu Skool shape with a backless silhouette that's made to be easy for on-the-go moments. It features a sculpted heel and custom artwork on the footbed, making these a truly special limited-edition gift idea for yourself or the SZA-lover you know.

Footwear highlights include SZA’s fresh take on two classic Vans styles. The Knu Skool Mule is a slip-on style that reimagines Vans’ ’90s-inspired Knu Skool with an easy-on-and-off shape and sculpted heel designed to help keep the foot in place, so you won’t walk out of them. Second, the Authentic Kickdown takes a different route: distressed canvas is covered with fish-print artwork—by artist Sage Adams—and features a collapsible heel to easily shift into a mule-style when on-the-go.

Ready to bring SZA’s outdoorsy, cool-girl energy to your cold-weather rotation? Explore the limited-edition VANSZA collection while select styles are still in stock.

Don't bug out! This fitted white tee features original artwork by Sage Adams and the custom VANSZA logo at the back. It’s an easy everyday staple with a little artsy energy.

This cool ball cap features flames made of RealTree camo print covering the classic logo. It has an adjustable snapback closure and a relaxed, slightly oversized fit—easy to throw on for bad hair days.

It's official, camo print is a trending pattern this winter, and this layered long-sleeve brings the trend into winter as a warm layering option. Wear it solo for a laid-back statement or layered under a jacket when the weather turns.

For winter, matching sweatsuit sets are an easy ensemble for looking put-together and keeping warm—so make them VANSZA for cool factor. This cozy hoodie with a kangaroo pocket is ready for slow mornings, a long playlist or any day when comfort is the whole mood.

Fashioned in a jogger silhouette with hand pockets, a high-rise and self-tie waistband, these oversized sweatpants feel fashionable, especially when worn as the set.

Exclusive to VANSZA, this Authentic shape has a playful fish print on its distressed canvas for a lived-in feel before you even slip them on. It's also designed with a collapsible heel, so you can wear them as a traditional lace-up or slip-on.

A simple, relaxed tee is always useful, and this one brings the VANSZA point of view to a simple outfit. Pair it with baggy denim or cargo pants for an easy, pulled-together look.

With an oversized, boxy fit, cargo pockets and a safety-orange lining, this gorp-core vest brings a bold utilitarian touch to a layered look. It’s a functional layering piece with actual personality.

SZA earns points for creativity with this crewneck that's printed to look like a worn-in work jacket. The trompe l’oeil print gives you the lived-in workwear feel with the comfort of a sweater. The matching pants are sold out, so don't miss your chance at the top.

Cargo pants are topping the trend cycel for this winter season and these are tje kind of jeans that make a simple tee-and-sneakers outfit feel intentional. Baggy, vintage-washed denim gets the pre-worn treatment with several cargo pockets and lived-in details.

Vintage-washed denim, oversized proportions and exaggerated pockets give this retro jacket a cool secondhand feel. The standout layer is a warm topper that says "my grind never stops."

Plaid and checked flannel toppers are a winter staple for good reason, and this layered style is substantial enough to brave the cold. The soft, thermal-lined hood and quilted interior make this an especially cozy take on a shirt-jacket hybrid. Elbow patches add to the well-loved, pre-broken-in feel.

A trouser that's too-cool-for-school with an oversized, cargo design clearly approved by SZA. These ripstop pants have plenty of pockets—including hidden stash pockets—and an adjustable drawstring waist. They’re a practical pick with a full-on statement silhouette.

#857. Should Premier League strugglers stick or twist as pressure on managers mounts? | Andrew Beasley

Unusually, all clubs in the top flight have the same manager with whom they began the season – but the first sacking may not be far away

No Premier League manager has yet lost his job this season. In only three of the past 10 campaigns was November reached without a club making a managerial change.

The 2026-27 season commencing with 11 managers who were appointed at some point in 2026 has probably contributed to the early season stability. They have to be given a chance to fashion their side as they see fit. But with roughly a quarter of the season played and only one more round of fixtures before an international break, the first sacking may not be far away.

Michael Carrick remains the favourite to be the next manager to leave his post. He is unsurprisingly followed by the managers of the clubs who occupy the relegation zone: Pierre Sage of Crystal Palace, Sunderland’s Régis Le Bris and Oliver Glasner at Nottingham Forest. It seems almost inevitable that Carrick will leave soon so the more interesting analysis lies among the bottom three.

Sunderland sit 20th and are predicted by Opta to finish there. However, they have had a testing start to the season. Le Bris’s side have faced five of the current top seven clubs, the joint-most along with Liverpool. The manager also has enormous reserves of goodwill after taking the club back to the Premier League and then into Europe.

Despite their tough schedule, Sunderland came into the weekend within one expected point of Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham before losing 3-1 at Coventry with the xG count 1.8 to 0.7 in their favour. It was a familiar outcome for a side that has scored 6.2 goals fewer than expected this season.

With Sunderland’s next five league opponents being Chelsea, Aston Villa, Tottenham, Liverpool and Newcastle, the challenge of staying up will not immediately get easier. At least their chance‑converting woes are not as bad as those of Nottingham Forest.

Their shots have been worth 14.7 expected goals, the fourth most in the division after the matches on Saturday. But not once in a game this season have the goals they scored at least equalled their xG, let alone surpassed it. It is a finishing issue, not a question of opposition goalkeepers having super-human performances against them.

The analytical step above standard expected goals is xG on target (xGOT). It measures the likelihood of an on-target shot becoming a goal based on chance quality and shot placement. Forest’s xGOT this season is 7.4, little more than half of their expected goal tally.

This inability to test goalkeepers severely enough explains why Glasner’s men have scored just six times. They are squandering almost one goal per game on average according to their expected goals, a significant shortfall. None of the 96 teams in Europe’s big five leagues were worse than 0.5 goals per match below xG last season, which suggests Forest’s luck should turn for the better.

Is Evangelos Marinakis patient enough for that to happen? Forest’s expected goal data is much stronger for Glasner than it was under any of the four managers their owner fired last season. Whether he pays attention to such numbers is a different issue.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Glasner hinted at a physical deficiency in the squad after defeat at Brentford. “We are outrun by the opposition in every single game. We have to change it,” he said. Distance covered data from Fotmob suggests that is not quite the case, albeit Forest have been outrun in their past five league games. Both the underlying xG data and physical statistics are worse at Glasner’s former club Crystal Palace though.

As expected goals have a far greater bearing on future performance or results than running stats, those numbers are the greater concern. Equally, Palace’s average of 96.9 sprints per match is the fewest in the Premier League (after Saturday’s matches).

The club have been through similar teething troubles with new managers before. Palace’s previous two appointments that occurred between seasons were Frank de Boer and Patrick Vieira. The former was sacked after only five matches in all competitions in 2017, the latter won just one of his first nine league games four years later before recovering to finish 12th.

While Palace are a little wasteful in attack, they have not been as bad as Forest or Sunderland. Their defence is a much bigger problem, which is unusual as Sage’s Lens conceded the fourth fewest expected goals in Ligue 1 last season. Palace are second worst for that metric in the Premier League in 2026‑27, rock bottom if penalties are excluded. Some of that may be down to starting seven combinations of players in the back three because of injuries and Axel Disasi’s three‑match ban, but it is imperative that a manager overcomes such inevitable difficulties.

Palace host Liverpool next weekend. They return after the international break with potentially winnable games against Coventry and Hull. Will those fixtures represent a good opportunity for Sage to kickstart his reign or an excellent chance for his replacement to hit the ground running? Only the chair, Steve Parish, will know the answer but Palace are the strugglers who look most in need of managerial change.

#854. Bill Belichick Shuts Down Question About Jordon Hudson Breakup

Days after it was confirmed that University of North Carolina coach Bill Belichick and Jordon Hudson had broken up, the NFL alum shut down a reporter’s question about the split.

Bill Belichick is throwing a flag on this play.

Days after it was confirmed that the University of North Carolina football coach and pro cheerleader Jordon Hudson had broken up last year, he shut down a question regarding the split.

“Do you work for a tabloid now?” Belichick asked a WRAL reporter during a press conference Nov. 2. “I'll keep my personal comments and relationships to myself if that's alright with you.”

Belichick’s question turnover comes after multiple outlets confirmed on Oct. 30 that the 74-year-old and 25-year-old had parted ways romantically, although reports noted they still maintain a close working relationship and friendship.

And while Hudson and Belichick have not invited the world into their huddle, the former pageant star has proved their friendship has not suffered any penalties by sticking by the New England Patriots alum. After all, the cheerleader was recently spotted on the sidelines of UNC’s Oct. 24 match-up against Syracuse, supporting Belichick through his team’s 31-30 loss.

Hudson and Belichick have even remained teammates away from the field. In May, Hudson shared a glimpse into the duo’s day at the Kentucky Derby, showing a photo of them walking hand-in-hand through Churchill Downs racetrack while sporting coordinated pink and blue attire.

Although recent reports have confirmed the former couple had already split up at that point, Hudson cheekily nodded to the backlash the couple had faced throughout their age gap relationship, captioning it, “Not the first time we’ve trudged through the mud together.”

A few days earlier, Hudson also shared a glimpse into Belichick supporting her at the Cheerleading Worlds competition in Orlando, Fla., writing in an April 26 Instagram post, “Roses up for Bill the WAG.”

Belichick and Hudson’s romance began in 2023, shortly after the NFL alum’s split from ex Linda Holliday. The duo went public with their romance in 2024, prompting many critical responses to their nearly 50-year age gap.

However, Hudson maintained a strong D-line when it came to defending the duo’s former romance.

"Nothing changed for us in 2024 except for 'public knowledge'; yet, somehow everything changed," Hudson wrote in a 2025 Instagram Story, which she later reshared earlier this year. “Fourth calendar year; Going strong. I can't wait to take punches for you in 2025.”

Hudson added in her post at the time, “Keep swinging, Keyboard Warriors. Your illusion of righteousness only fuels my authenticity.”

For more couples who have called it quits recently, keep reading…

In October, multiple outlets confirmed that the eight-time Super Bowl-winning coach, 74, and former Bridgewater State University cheerleader, 25, ended their relationship in late 2025 after about four years of dating.

The Selling Sunset alum shared an emotional video announcement confirming that she and the Australian musician “are no longer together” three years after tying the knot in 2023.

“We have agreed to treat this public separation with love and respect for each other," Chrishell said in an Instagram post Oct. 26. "That’s not hard for me because I am in love with this person.”

The Friday Night Lights alum and the Imagine Dragons member broke up after almost four years together, according to multiple outlets.

The two had confirmed their romance in November 2022 and made their official red carpet debut on May 30, 2026.

Three months after confirming they were separated, the Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star filed for divorce in Utah.

The trailer for the seventh season of RHOSLC revealed just how strained the relationship between the Wild Rose Beauty founder and her husband had become.

The Hills alum confirmed her romance with the "Whiskey and Rain" singer had ended after two years of dating.

The "Mi Gente" singer (real name José Álvaro Osorio Balvín) and the model broke up after nearly 10 years of dating.

"After sharing so many years and important moments together, Jose and I have decided to go our separate ways," Ferrer wrote on her instagram Story Sept. 16. "It has been a decision made out of love, respect, and the desire to do the best for our family."

Noting that co-parenting son Rio "with all our love" is top priority, she added, "We are living this process with ease and deeply appreciate the understanding and respect towards this time so personal to us."

“We have been separated for a while, and it’s proven to be the right move for us and our family unit," the Mean Girls alum and the Newsroom actor told People in a joint statement Sept. 15. "We’ve got each other forever—and it’s GOOD."

On Aug. 19, multiple outlets reported that the Fifty Shades of Grey star and the "Sally, When the Wine Runs Out" singer broke up less than one year after sparking dating rumors.

The Fashion Police alum confirmed her split from the musician amid reports that he had been fired from Slipknot, writing on Instagram Stories Aug. 3, "Strange how the loudest defense of the guilty is rarely innocence… It’s distraction."

"I will not take your s--t anymore! I’m done,” she added. "Leave me alone. Let me heal. I can’t protect you from yourself anymore."

The Empire actress confirmed the former couple had called off their engagement and ended their three-year relationship in a lengthy Instagram statement.

"I loved deeply," Serayah wrote in the Aug. 25 post. "Believed wholeheartedly in the life we were building, and wanted nothing more than to protect our family."

The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star and her husband separated after 16 years of marriage, multiple outlets reported in July.

“It has been a sad and difficult situation, but we have been focused on navigating the change privately and positively for a healthy and happy co parenting environment for our son, and ourselves,” the pair—parents to Sky Safir Cornish Colman—shared in a July 20 statement. “Unfortunately being in the public eye this is the easiest way to let people know the truth, before rumours circulate or a false narrative is written.”

After nearly seven years of marriage, E! News confirmed July 16 that the Ozark actress and Foster the People frontman had split. Though the pair did not immediately speak publicly on their breakup, they wiped their Instagram accounts of their pictures together.

Nearly three decades after tying the knot, The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star and her husband have separated, according to multiple outlets.

The pair, who share 15-year-old daughter Elektra, tied the knot in June 1999 and have since built a hair salon empire, which they co-own.

After the Las Culturistas podcast host and Below Deck star began dating in the summer of 2025 following an Instagram meet-cute, E! News confirmed July 16 that the pair mutually decided to part ways and remain friends.

The Malcolm in the Middle star shared that he and Price were splitting up after six years of marriage.

“After 10 beautiful years together, we’ve grown in ways that made us realize our relationship feels most natural and strong as a deep friendship and as co-parents,” Muniz and Price wrote in a joint Instagram post July 1. “We share an incredible son who remains the center of our world, and we’re both happier, stronger parents because of the love and growth we’ve shared.”

The two welcomed son Mauz Mosley Muniz in March 2021.

The White Stripes frontman's wife of four years filed for divorce on June 3 in Nashville, citing "irreconcilable differences and inappropriate marital conduct" as the reason for breakup, per court documents obtained by E! News.

The "Amen" singer filed for divorce from the Dumb Blonde podcast host after nearly 10 years of marriage on May 18, according to court records obtained by E! News.

The pair denied cheating was involved, sharing that they remain on good terms. In fact, Bunnie said she and Jelly Roll are "still having a baby" together after embarking on an IVF journey years ago.

After nearly three years together, the former Wicked costars' split was confirmed in June, with a source telling E! News it was "amicable" and they had been separated "for months."

The fitness trainer confirmed that she and the former MLB star had broken up after three years of dating.

"To clarify, Alex and I are currently taking some time apart but there continues to be mutual love, care, and deep respect between us and for our families," Jaclyn told TMZ in a May statement. "We remain supportive of one another, and there is absolutely no animosity, drama, or negative story here."

The Grey’s Anatomy alum confirmed in May that she and her husband—who share kids Noah, Taeyln and Anniston—quietly broke up after more than two decades of marriage.

After nearly 20 years of marriage, the American Pie star and the Angel alum split, their rep confirmed to E! News May 14.

Despite ending their romance the couple's rep emphasized the remain on "great terms" and are committed to coparenting their sons Sid and Lazlo.

"I've made the decision to end my relationship with Klay," the rapper told E! News in an April 25 statement. "Trust, fidelity and respect are non-negotiable for me in a relationship, and when those values are compromised, there's no real path forward."

The statement came shortly after Megan accused the NBA star of cheating, writing on her Instagram Story, "Holding you down through all your HORRIBLE mood swings and treatment towards me during your basketball season now you don't know if you can be 'monogamous'????"

The Material Girls actress and her fiancé called it quits after 14 years together.

The estranged couple share daughters Ryan, born in 2015, and Lulu, born in 2018.

The soccer legend and WNBA star, who met preparing while preparing for the 2016 Rio Olympics, announced their breakup in April.

“After a lot of thought, we've made the decision to separate as a couple,” they wrote in a joint statement shared to Instagram April 17. “This hasn't been an easy decision, but it's one we've made together, with so much love, respect, and care for each other.”

Megan and Sue added, “We've shared a whole life over the last decade, through big moments and in quiet ones, and that is something we'll always carry with us.”

The Real Housewives of New York star's husband filed for divorce on April 2 after nine years of marriage, according to a court docket viewed by E! News.

In the filing, David is listed as the plaintiff, filing for a summons and complaint, or instigation of a lawsuit. Sai—mom to London and Rio with David—is listed as the defendant and has yet to address the filing publicly.

Sai joined RHONY in its 2023 recast season and addressed rumors that she “stole” her husband from his previous wife while on the reality show.

“I met David six years after he got a divorce,” Sai said during the ninth episode of season 15. “I have his divorce paperwork.”

The Pretty Little Liars alum and her husband quietly split after seven years of marriage, a source with knowledge confirmed to E! News April 10.

Five months after the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star admitted to an emotional affair with Vanderpump Villa star Marciano Brunette, her husband filed for divorce, according to Utah court records viewed by E! News.

"This has not been an easy decision and it comes with a heavy heart,” he told TMZ in a March 19 statement. “I’m grateful for the shared memories and the lessons. While our paths are now moving in different directions, my priority remains my children and ensuring they feel loved, supported, and protected through this transition."

Two years after getting engaged, the Los Angeles Lakers point guard announced the couple's breakup, sharing that he is focusing on their daughters Gabriela and Olivia.

“I love my daughters more than anything and I've been doing everything I can for them to be with me in the U.S. during the season, but that hasn't been possible,” Luka said in a statement to ESPN March 10, “so I recently made the tough decision to end my engagement.”

“Everything I do is for my daughters' happiness,” he continued, “and I will always fight to be with them and give them the best life I can.”

Prior to Luca speaking out, Anamaria filed a legal petition in California seeking child support and attorney’s fees, according to court documents obtained by E! News.

After being engaged since October 2024, the Dallas Cowboys quarterback's fiancée shared she was “heartbroken” to be breaking up.

"There wasn’t any rockiness in the lead up, and there was no big argument or blow up,” a rep for Sarah Jane told People in a statement March 9. “It was a mutual decision.”

As such, the former couple, who share daughters Margaret and Aurora are looking ahead at their co-parenting journey.

#853. US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors

As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.

On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.

The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.

Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.

For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.

It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.

The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.

Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.

Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.

Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.

"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.

Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.

That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.

For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.

Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.

"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."

The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.

Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.

Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.

Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.

"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.

That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.

Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.

Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

#852. Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

Marco Rose’s tactics are lifting Bournemouth, Roméo Lavia makes progress with Chelsea and Roberto De Zerbi gives youth a chance at Spurs

Good defending is the mark of champions. At Anfield, where Arsenal had not won in the past 13 visits, Mikel Arteta followed the orthodoxy of locking down once his team took the lead. This time around, it proved successful. Arsenal did not allow the occasion or the stadium to get to them as they have on previous occasions. In April 2023, Granit Xhaka entangling with Trent Alexander-Arnold energised home fans previously despondent that Arsenal were 2-0 up. It finished 2-2. On Sunday, Liverpool zipped around zestfully, as Andoni Iraola requests, though the final-ball quality was lacking. That owed a great deal to the organisation of the Arsenal defence. Ahead of the last international break, Brighton set a blueprint for getting the better of Arsenal in winning 3-0. Liverpool’s squad profile might have made a similar strategy possible though Iraola’s outfit is struggling to create chances in the same volume as Brighton or his Bournemouth team. John Brewin

No shots on target for Liverpool, leaving them with zero margin for the errors that preceded Kai Havertz’s decisive goal. Nine points behind Arsenal with a quarter of the season gone, Liverpool’s season risks becoming a developmental one, a time to regroup and rethink rather than challenging for the title. The squad Iraola inherited still bears the weight of the failed rebuild of the summer of 2025. Florian Wirtz was both unlucky when rattling the crossbar and too ponderous when a second-half chance dropped his way. Alexander Isak is nothing like the busy-bee striker his manager asks to press from the front. Milos Kerkez continues to be chaotic. Bradley Barcola, 2026’s headline signing, played his part in the flurry that followed Arsenal’s goal but faded, as did his fellow forwards. There are shards of light. Jérémy Jacquet and Trey Nyoni (aggressive – perhaps too aggressive – and involved in his hour on the field) are young players who can go places. Though it may take some time for Liverpool to get there as a team. JB

Reaction: Iraola responds to Isak penalty denial

The small matter of a glamorous trip to Barcelona comes first for Aston Villa but it is a quirk of timing that Unai Emery’s next Premier League assignment should come at Old Trafford. It is the historical stature of Manchester United that triggered all the controversy over Jamie Carragher’s claim that Emery should be looking to climb the football chain and consider succeeding Michael Carrick should he be sacked. But even if Emery perceived United as a step up (as Youri Tielemans did when trading clubs in the summer, and look where that’s led him), would he prosper there? At Villa Park, he has an increasingly strong hold on how all team affairs are run, as signalled by his nominal upgrade from head coach to manager when he last signed a new contract, and he will visit the Camp Nou looking to extend Villa’s 100% start to their Champions League campaign. Having suffered dips at Paris Saint-Germain and Arsenal, there is no certainty Emery’s methods would work in the febrile cauldron that is Old Trafford. After all, Manchester United will never be Aston Villa. Peter Lansley

Bournemouth are in full flow, winning each of their past six matches, scoring 16 goals. All while Alex Scott is absent with the muscle injury sustained with England. Those goals have come unanswered. Marco Rose has added a defensive solidity not always present during Iraola’s era. Last season’s goal difference was +4. Djordje Petrovic has not conceded a goal since the 5-1 defeat at Chelsea on 10 October. “The Chelsea game was the moment we changed all momentum,” said Petrovic after beating Leeds. Rose has admitted testing opening weeks in the Premier League had altered perceptions to force a rethink. “Everyone in the team, starting from the attackers, is doing their job offensively and defensively,” Petrovic said. Since Stamford Bridge, commitment to the collective has paid impressive dividends. “If you have that intensity with the attackers, it gets easier, we have a good group of players with quality and huge rotations in each position.” JB

Match report: Bournemouth 2-0 Leeds United

Roméo Lavia completed his first 90 minutes as a Chelsea player during their Carabao Cup defeat by Liverpool last Wednesday. It was a major milestone for a player who has struggled to stay fit since joining from Southampton three years ago. Lavia’s injury record invites caution but the midfielder is making progress. He followed up his performance against Liverpool with his second consecutive 90-minute display when Chelsea beat Manchester United 2-0 on Saturday. “As long as I feel good, I’ll do everything possible to help the team to get this type of result and I’m feeling good, so I’m very happy with my performance,” Lavia said after starring against United and creating the opening goal for Morgan Rogers. “All I can say is that the work that we’re doing with all the people at the club is going well. It’s just about keeping it going. Hopefully it can continue this way.” Jacob Steinberg

Match report: Chelsea 2-0 Manchester United

With Tottenham cruising towards a third successive Premier League victory, against 10-man Crystal Palace, Roberto De Zerbi decided the time had come in the 88th minute. Luca Williams-Barnett is rated as one of the best prospects to emerge from the Spurs academy in many years but the attacking midfielder has had to be patient for his first league appearance as De Zerbi’s side struggled at the start of the season. The 18-year-old made an instant impression with a sensational first touch and pass after replacing Mathys Tel before setting up Mohammed Kudus for a great chance, to make it 3-0, that was spurned. We can expect to see more of him if De Zerbi gets his way. “My career is clear: when I have young, talented players, nothing changes,” he said. “I thought it was the right moment for him in the Premier League – but as a quality, he’s a big, big talent.” Ed Aarons

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Match report: Tottenham 2-0 Crystal Palace

After Fabian Hürzeler masterminded Brighton’s fine 1-0 win at Manchester City that lifted the Seagulls to 19 points, only two behind their hosts, the manager pointed to the culture he is building. “For me, I think it’s a lot about connection. We work in the people business. And we speak a lot about players. But for me, it’s more important to understand the person behind the player. And therefore, we try to build a lot on connection. We try to build a lot on culture. Because I think having the right values, having the right connection, the right relationship between the players helps you massively on the pitch. On the pitch, they need to rely on each other, trust each other. And you can only build this on and off the pitch. And therefore, we try to emphasise this a lot.” Jamie Jackson

Match report: Manchester City 0-1 Brighton

The oddity about Brentford this season is that they’re playing well, have a very good chance of qualifying for Europe for the first time in their history, and yet there’s been a feeling that they’ve been leaving points behind. Inexplicably, victory over Nottingham Forest was their first win in five and their first clean sheet since the 3-0 demolition of Chelsea six weeks ago. Perhaps the biggest issue in terms of improving on last season’s ninth-placed finish was whether Igor Thiago could match his tally of 22 goals. He’s started this campaign slowly, but got his second of the season with Brentford’s second against Forest. The finish, which looped in off Nikola Milenkovic, was fortuitous and not entirely convincing, but more significant perhaps was the way he stepped back away from the defenders, creating space for Jaidon Anthony to pick him out. That instinct will always generate chances, and the finishing will surely return. Jonathan Wilson

Match report: Brentford 2-0 Nottingham Forest

The word at Ipswich is that Julio Enciso has come back to the club with an increased level of maturity after a year in Ligue 1. He occasionally sparkled at Portman Road on loan from Brighton in the second half of the doomed 2024-25 season but lacked consistency. This season he already has two goals, a pair of assists and has become Ipswich’s chief creator. Enciso is comfortably top of the club’s chances-created chart, the Paraguayan’s tally of 14 is nearly double the next names on the list – Sasa Lukic, Emersonn and Abdul Fatawu, who have eight apiece. After the Tractor Boys had managed to turn a 1-0 lead into a 2-1 deficit at Hull, Enciso’s thwack from the edge of the box earned his side a vital point. He will be required to keep producing these kinds of moments if Gary O’Neil’s side are to do what they couldn’t last time around and stay in the top flight for consecutive seasons. Tom Bassam

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said post-match: “First year in Europe, you will have on average 10 less points. It’s our reality.” The reality is Sunderland have 12 points fewer than they did after nine games last season and if you extrapolate their current form over 38 games it amounts to relegation. Only Crystal Palace have conceded more goals and only Nottingham Forest have scored fewer. It would stun no one to learn that those three clubs make up the bottom three, but what is a surprise is that three promoted sides are all looking capable of avoiding the drop. A word for Coventry, who have responded to a chastening start to the season by winning three of their past five. Beating the teams around you is important in the fight for survival and this was a big tick in that box. TB

#851. Earth’s resources sustain humanity — but they come at a high price

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Richard Schiffman is an environmental journalist in New York City.

A huge lithium-mining operation in Chile’s Atacama Desert.Credit: AP Photo/Rodrigo Abd/Alamy

The Elements of Life: How Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium Nourish Us and Threaten the Planet Kerstin Hoppenhaus Greystone (2026)

The Vanishing Earth: Dispatches from the Frontiers of Extraction James Crawford Bloomsbury (2026)

For much of human history, our species has treated Earth as an inexhaustible source of raw materials. In the past half-century, people have taken more resources from the natural world than in our entire previous history. And the rate of extraction is rising as the global population grows.

Oil and gas drilling is shifting to the deep sea — here’s what is at stake

Oil and gas drilling is shifting to the deep sea — here’s what is at stake

Two books argue that we need to put the brakes on our unsustainable use of resources. In The Vanishing Earth, historian and journalist James Crawford recounts his travels to five landscapes that have been reshaped by drilling and mining.

And, in The Elements of Life, science journalist Kerstin Hoppenhaus examines the three elements vital for plant growth: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Both books are informative and non-technical primers on humanity’s ever-increasing use of Earth’s dwindling resources.

Crawford developed an early interest in the impacts of mining as the son of a mechanical engineer who worked in extractive industries around the world, from the coal beds of Scotland to copper mines in Zambia and oil rigs in the North Sea. He is far from being the first to raise such concerns. First-century Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder wrote of how mining operations “urge us to our ruin” and wondered “when will be the end of thus exhausting the earth”.

Today’s industrial mining operations are on a scale Pliny could have hardly imagined, creating vast toxic areas called sacrifice zones that are, in some cases, uninhabitable. Crawford observed this at first hand when he visited the salt flats of the Atacama Desert in Chile, one of the world’s largest reserves of lithium. Lithium batteries are used in technologies from smartphones to electric vehicles, and demand for the element is expected to rise 50-fold by 2040, which would far outstrip our current ability to extract it.

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

In Chile, Crawford reports signs that the brine that is the source of lithium salts is already running out, threatening the wider ecosystem with collapse. Indigenous communities in the area are also finding that their water sources are drying up as mining activities deplete reserves stored in the underlying aquifer. The vast Salar de Atacama wetland, which is inhabited by three species of flamingo, might soon become a dead zone, unable to support aquatic life.

Some of the most common resources are also the most overexploited, the author contends. Global demand for clean water has doubled since 1960 and it is predicted that, by the middle of this century, nearly two-thirds of the world’s population will experience water stress, as intensive agriculture depletes aquifers and droughts become more frequent because of climate change. In cities, especially in arid areas, these problems can be exacerbated. Nearly all of China’s major cities are sinking because of subsidence resulting from aquifer depletion, and water shortages have imperilled cities from São Paulo in Brazil to Cape Town in South Africa. Such pressures have inspired schemes to tow icebergs from polar regions, but none has yet been implemented. Failure to tackle these issues could have catastrophic consequences. Struggles over water are projected to become a source of global conflict: water was once dubbed “the petroleum of the next century” in a report by the investment firm Goldman Sachs.

After water, sand is the world’s second most widely used resource. Crawford finds that it is also being over-extracted, as beaches worldwide are mined to meet the demand for construction concrete, which uses sand as its main ingredient. In Vietnam’s Mekong River Delta, intensive sand removal has caused whole sections of coastal farmland to collapse into the river and the ocean. Sand extraction in Sri Lanka has destroyed beaches, exacerbating the impact of sea-level rise and increasing the destructive power of the deadly 2004 tsunami. In India, illegal sand-mining operations have become so lucrative that they are a mainstay of organized crime.

The end of phosphate mining in Nauru has left behind a barren landscape of pinnacles.Credit: Auscape/UIG/Getty

Oil and other fossil fuels are unlikely to run out any time soon, but continued drilling poses a threat to biodiversity and human health. In the Ecuadorian jungle, for example, Crawford describes how chemicals released by drilling have caused cancer rates in the worst polluted areas to rise precipitously. In 2023, Ecuador became the first country where a citizen referendum voted to keep the oil in the ground, after previously becoming the first nation to grant legal rights to the natural world. Nevertheless, drilling continues for now in Ecuador, which, Crawford writes, has “tied its entire fate to oil”.

What can be done? Some environmental damage is inevitable when natural resources are extracted, but Crawford calls for a “repair revolution” to restore blighted landscapes. There is no such thing as “sustainable extraction”, he writes, but there must be “life … after extraction”.

#849. Goals, guests and 6,561 scenarios: inside ESPN on the biggest NWSL Decision Day yet

The final day of the regular season gave fans Gotham’s Shield win, a farewell to a Seattle hero and a new part-whiparound, part-watchalong show to take it all in

As a player, Ali Krieger went into NWSL Decision Day focused on one result. She was Gotham FC’s captain in 2023, the first time the league played all of the final games of the regular season simultaneously. The job, she remembers, was to not worry about the other games going on.

Three years later, Krieger spent Decision Day with eyes on not one game but eight. For the first time, all of the final games of the NWSL season were aired by the same network. Krieger, now a lead analyst for ESPN, and host Kelsey Riggs Cuff anchored the coverage from headquarters in Bristol with a show that was part whiparound, part watchalong, and ultimately wholly new for the 14-year-old league.

There was no shortage of storylines. With 16 teams in action, the slate of simultaneous kickoffs was the largest in the league’s history. San Diego and Gotham were fighting for the Shield; four teams were jousting for home-field advantage; three were vying for the final playoff spots. The league simulated Sunday’s games 50,000 times and found more than 200 possibilities for playoff brackets, with 6,561 ways the results could go.

How do you prepare for the way that the story does spin? The network deployed 60-plus cameras and more than 150 staffers around the United States, plus about 20 in Bristol. Cuff and Krieger met with researchers, rewatched games and assembled a 12-page Google Doc of notes.

“You know that it’s going to be chaos. You lean into the breaking news feel of it,” Cuff said in the green room, about an hour before the games began. “And then you just sit back and enjoy it, because this is the biggest day that we have on the calendar right now, with so much on the line from top to bottom.”

First-place Gotham’s home match against Utah was the headliner on ESPN’s main channel, with the other seven on the streaming service ESPN+ and Krieger and Cuff’s studio show on ESPN2. It wasn’t ESPN’s first time producing a whiparound-style soccer studio show – the network has done so for the Bundesliga and US Open Cup – but it was the first for the NWSL.

“This is like a fresh canvas,” said Manuel de la Fe, vice-president of production at ESPN. “We’re going to paint, and we’re going to see how it comes out.”

A mantra for live television is to expect the unexpected, and the hosts quickly learned Sunday that the unexpected includes surprise women’s college volleyball upsets. A Tennessee-Missouri five-setter meant the start of the Gotham match was pushed to the ESPN2 slot, and the studio show did not actually begin until about 25 minutes into the games.

By the time it kicked into gear, there was plenty to talk about. San Diego, in second place and facing Bay FC in San Jose, scored the day’s first goal in the ninth minute; Gotham scored in their own game seconds later.

For those who prefer their whiparound shows to have the cadence of NFL RedZone’s rollercoaster, this wasn’t exactly that. Earlier Sunday, Krieger mentioned Diana Taurasi and Sue Bird’s women’s basketball watchalongs as inspiration for this show, and it called on special guests in the style of the Manningcast.

While the interviews did occasionally push the game action itself off screen, they also provided some of the day’s highlights. Lead reporter Jeff Kassouf added insights into the changing table. Olivia Moultrie, recovering from an ACL injury, reacted live as her Portland Thorns scored their first goal. Megan Rapinoe called in from a suite at Seattle’s Lumen Field. (“I’m not in the closet, but I am in the bathroom,” Rapinoe quipped.)

There were still some snafus. During the Portland game, the feed cut while Sophia Wilson was in the run-up to a penalty kick, jumping to an interview with Heather O’Reilly and a stream of the North Carolina game. Some viewers online spoke of audio-synching issues in certain games.

But after just six first-half goals across the eight games, the second half brought more action. Angel City poured three goals on Boston Legacy; Washington scored while their game was in a triple-box display. The show popped into the Seattle match and captured the Reign’s go-ahead goal, vital for their playoff hopes. A poignant moment came 14 minutes later, when Jess Fishlock subbed off and a national audience could watch the farewell of an NWSL icon.

“When you’re in it, there’s so much pressure to be able to perform and apply everything you’ve worked towards,” said Krieger who, like Fishlock, played the final regular-season minutes of her career on a Decision Day. “There’s a different fire that comes out in players when there’s something to fight for more than just a win.”

It has been a mixed time for the NWSL’s media deal, which was valued at $60m per season upon signing in 2023 and runs through the 2027 campaign. The league had to drop one partner, Victory+, because of the streamer’s missed payments, and the fragmented slate forces viewers to pay for many platforms. But there’s also been marked growth. Across four Women’s Sports Sundays telecasts on ESPN, the soccer matches averaged 255,000 viewers, up 106% against the regular-season average last year. NWSL viewership is up on all three of ESPN’s linear platforms.

Of the possible scenarios, the one that played out was not the most dramatic, but it was a satisfying close. Gotham became first-time Shield winners; Kansas City and Washington ensured their home quarter-finals; Seattle clinched the final playoff spot; and Utah secured theirs for the first time in club history.

Gotham’s Shield lift, with the backdrop of fireworks and their home fans at Sports Illustrated Stadium, made for an apt closing visual. (Had San Diego jumped Gotham to win, they would have received medals in San Jose, then the sterling silver trophy next week.)

The crew at ESPN signed off, posed for some pictures and then turned to work on the next assignment: sorting out plans for the playoffs, which begin Friday.

#848. Defeat for London City - but is Europe a real possibility?

Clinical Man City edge past London City in WSL thriller

It shows how quickly London City Lionesses have progressed that they were hugely disappointed with a narrow defeat by defending champions Manchester City.

For a team that were playing second-tier football 18 months ago, their lofty ambitions of qualifying for the Champions League suddenly don't seem far-fetched.

London City looked like the better team for most of the afternoon at Hayes Lane but were given a harsh lesson by the visitors in how to be ruthless.

Manchester City needed goals from Khadija Shaw and Lauren Hemp against the run of play, but they dug in to win 2-1 and to continue setting the pace at the top of the Women's Super League.

Those goals came after countless opportunities went begging for London City, who ended the game having had 24 shots but only six on target.

The performance was enough, however, to show that London City are more than capable of competing with the WSL's elite.

The next question is whether they can do it consistently.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

London City Lionesses are a club who do things differently and, backed by US billionaire Michele Kang, they are not shy to disrupt the current order.

They are an independent women's football club who have spent big in the transfer window and agreed a record-breaking shirt deal with Nike believed to be worth more than Â£3m a year.

They have built their own training facility in Kent and persuaded superstars such as Alexia Putellas to join in the summer.

Spain international Putellas showcased her latest Ballon d'Or trophy - the third of her career - before kick-off on Sunday.

London City Lionesses are clearly no minnows, but even a squad full of superstars needs time to gel.

It was for this reason that people doubted whether they were ready this season to qualify for the Champions League and break the WSL's traditional top three.

But on Sunday's showing, they are not as far off as people thought.

Manager Eder Maestre said the team's performances are already at the level they want but results have not always shown that and they still have work to do.

"That's why it's a very frustrating situation. We were speaking a lot about respecting the identity and it doesn't matter the team that we were facing," the Spaniard said.

"The next step in that project was showing everybody that we can perform, while respecting that identity that we are trying to build on.

"That's why it's doubly frustrating, because I think the result was not the one we deserve. Manchester City are more mature.

"They are more used to it. When you have this consistency and you are very used to playing these kinds of games, maybe you have more experience.

"That's why we have extra nervousness in the moments that we need to be more clinical."

Where London City fell was where Manchester City stood tall.

Moments of brilliance by world-class players Shaw and Hemp delivered the goods and when London City's pressure grew, so too did Manchester City's resilience.

It is that consistency across 90 minutes, and the season as a whole, that Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz believes will demonstrate the difference.

"They are a very good team and they really showed the highest level," said Jeglertz.

"What it means to be at the top of this league, is playing week after week, and at the same level - and finding different levels to win.

"That is what we have created. That's what everybody who wants to win something needs to be able to do. To contest, you need to compete for the whole season."

London City Lionesses dominated the first half as shown by the momentum swings

London City Lionesses are providing plenty of optimism on the pitch, but even if they were to qualify for the Champions League this season, are they allowed to?

Current Uefa rules state that owners cannot have two clubs competing in the same competition, meaning one of Kang's Lyon or London City Lionesses would potentially miss out.

It is a dilemma that many have discussed, but if they continue to perform so well, it could prove to be a problem earlier than expected.

"First of all, what we feel is important, is to be part of the conversation," London City's chief executive officer Martin Semmens told BBC Sport.

"The next stage is getting towards trophies. Our ambition is to be in Europe, to play in Europe every year, and to compete with the likes of Barcelona and Arsenal.

"We're probably one step behind that in squad development and all the other things we have to do. But on our day, we feel we can beat them."

London City's ambitions are clear - so what happens if they do qualify this season?

"I think Michele [Kang] has a really clear view and that is that she wants to see as much investment come into the women's game as possible," added Semmens.

"The men's multi-club ownership rules is about being careful not to have control over two clubs. We see it differently on the women's side.

"We want to see more investment, so we believe if you invest in more than one club, the game will accelerate faster.

"We truly understand and respect the rules, always. But there are logical, structured ways that we can compete in Europe next season."

#847. I'll tell my players to dive in future - Iraola

Arsenal move clear at the top with a rare win at Liverpool

Andoni Iraola says that he will tell his players to go down in future after Liverpool were denied a penalty in Sunday's defeat by Arsenal.

With Liverpool trailing 1-0 after Kai Havertz's opener, Alexander Isak's shirt was pulled by Jurrien Timber in the first half as he went for a header from Bradley Barcola's cross.

However, the Liverpool striker stayed on his feet and referee Andy Madley did not point to the spot.

Stuart Attwell, on video assistant referee (VAR) duty, determined that there was not enough in the tug for the decision to be overturned, but Iraola disagreed.

"There is a clear grab of the shirt," the Spaniard told Match of the Day. "Alex [Isak] was just in front of him, he was going to head in front of the goal but couldn't because he grabbed the shirt.

"If he goes to the floor, they call the penalty 100%. It should be like this but it is what it is. Next time, the managers should tell Alex to go to the floor, otherwise they won't call it.

"The answer is you have to dive, if you don't dive they won't call it."

Isak turned and spoke to Timber after the incident, but did not appeal to the referee after staying on his feet.

Iraola told Sky Sports that he believes managers should tell their players to go to the floor.

Asked if he will tell Isak that, he added: "Yes, definitely."

He elaborated in his news conference when asked by BBC Sport if he would have to tell his players to be more smart.

"It's a shame you ask me this question, but honestly, yes, we have to tell them, go down, because they're not going to call it otherwise. And then referees complain why they go down. Because if you don't go down, you don't call it. Then it's like, no, you are all the time going down," said Iraola.

"But I think Alex is honest. He tries to go for the ball, everyone can see live straight away that there is a clear, clear pull."

The understanding is that because there was minimal contact and it was a slight tug on the shirt, rather than a sustained holding offence, the play was allowed to continue.

Iraola conceded in his news conference that "it is not going to change anything" if Pro Ref, the Premier League's refereeing body, was to offer an apology about the incident.

Former Premier League assistant referee Darren Cann told BBC Sport: "Timber takes a huge risk by grabbing the shirt. It could easily have been given on another day.

"It's right on the limit. It has to be sustained holding - some will say it was sustained, some will say it wasn't. But it's interesting that Isak didn't even appeal."

Liverpool also had another penalty appeal turned waved away when Cody Gakpo went down in the box under pressure from Christos Tzolis.

Were Arsenal lucky not to give away a penalty?

From Fleetwood embarrassment to 'magical' Anfield win 14 years in making

Andoni Iraola post-match interview - Liverpool v Arsenal

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy said the decision came at a pivotal point in the game.

"I think Arsenal got lucky," he told Match of the Day. "If Isak maybe makes a bit more of it. I hate to see players exaggerate, but he's going to score. It's a big moment in the game

"I feel for the referee because it happened so quickly. I thought there was enough for VAR to have another look and give him another look. If he made more of it, maybe they would have given it on-field."

Gary Neville agreed that, for a centre-forward, it was an unusual reaction from Isak, who failed to connect with the ball due to the pull.

"The argument around Isak and whether he should have made more of it, it's unnatural not to make more of it," he said on Sky during commentary of the game.

"When you get pulled and you're just about to score a goal, you normally complain like crazy. It'd a very odd reaction from Isak not to react."

Asked if Isak should have reacted more, Liverpool skipper Virgil van Dijk said: "We have 50 cameras. Why does he have to complain when there are so many cameras. Everyone has seen it. In the end it wasn't given and we lose the game unfortunately, so well done to Arsenal."

#846. Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or party gives way to anxiety-filled hangover for Bayern Munich | Andy Brassell

Dortmund did not read the script, remaining level on points with the defending champions at the top of the table

It was the moment they had all been … not so much waiting for, but planning, pushing and yearning for. In the videos that announce the starting lineup on the giant scoreboard before kick-off, every Bayern Munich player turns to face the camera with their personal salute, greeting or goal celebration, the playful progression from the standard folding of arms. Except on Saturday evening, the No 9 turned around smiling, and cradling the golden trophy.

In the midweek DFB Pokal stroll against Magdeburg there had been a salute, the players welcoming Harry Kane on to the pitch with a guard of honour to commemorate his Ballon d’Or victory two nights before. This, however, was the real party, the moment where the England captain’s and Bayern’s successful union and the apex it has reached was celebrated in front of a global audience. There was every reason to believe it would be a full and satisfying victory lap, even in Der Klassiker, with proper competition so often bringing the best out of the Rekordmeister.

Dortmund, however, did not read the script. Neither did the football gods. Kane was not completely neutered in this and laid on yet another assist, nodding across goal to present Dayot Upamecano a second goal in successive Bundesliga games That looked like the winner until Fábio Silva’s 89th-minute equaliser for the visitors. Yet in between, there was frustration for the man who has walked on water since arriving in Munich. He clattered a penalty which could have made it 2-0 against the crossbar and hit the post from point-blank range when he could have made it 3-1, after Serhou Guirassy’s first equaliser and the Upamecano strike that put Bayern back in front.

Three years ago on Wednesday, Kane hit a hat-trick in his first Klassiker in a 4-0 win at Signal Iduna Park. Despite the cliche that BVB are Bayern’s bunnies, the champions have not had it all their own way in this fixture. This was Kane’s fourth Klassiker at the Allianz Arena, and Bayern have only won one of them. Many of those watching from around the world who tuned in to see Kane lift his personal trophy would have expected a subsequent procession to victory but having arrived level on points at the top of the table, Dortmund were able to leave Bavaria in the same position.

This was, as Ruhr Nachrichten’s Kevin Pinnow put it, “much more than just a point” for Dortmund. It was not a signal they are Bayern’s equal but a sign they could roll with the punches, that they could show guts and enterprise and find solutions, from the switch to a back four that blind-sided their hosts to the energy and daring in midfield, exemplified by Jobe Bellingham’s best performance since he arrived last year. The young Englishman is a symbol of the good Niko Kovac has done since arriving at the club, a combination of patience and high demand. The coach insisted earlier this year that Bellingham, despite a lack of numerical reward, was progressing ahead of schedule and this, finally was the proof. He might even have put BVB in front in the first half, but had a goal ruled out as the offside Carney Chukwuemeka – who also excelled – inadvertently stumbled into Jonas Urbig in the Bayern goal. “He is someone for the big stake,” enthused the sporting director, Ole Book. “He showed that today.”

SV Elversberg 4-1 Mainz, Augsburg 1-2 Freiburg, Mönchengladbach 0-0 Paderborn, Schalke 0-2 RB Leipzig, Werder 2-0 Hoffenheim, Leverkusen 2-4 VfB Stuttgart, Bayern 2-2 Dortmund, Union Berlin 1-1 Köln, Eintracht Frankfurt 3-1 Hamburg

Yet as worthy as Dortmund were, little went for Bayern. The bad luck was not limited to plural pinging of aluminium and the effects will last for longer than Monday morning. Already without Vincent Kompany, who will not be rushed back into action after his recent hospitalisation with his assistant, Aaron Danks, holding the fort, the injury list is getting out of hand. Danks went into this fixture without Luis Díaz, Manuel Neuer and Jamal Musiala and lost a further three forward players during the course of the evening.

Ismael Saibari injured his ankle ligaments in a collision with Gregor Kobel and has already had surgery, with the recovery to last at least three months. Serge Gnabry is expected to miss several weeks with a hamstring injury he picked up and, worst of all, Michael Olise went down off the ball with what appeared to be a knee problem in the closing minutes. Bayern will go into this week’s Champions League game with Atlético Madrid – surely the last game they would wish to face with a banged-up squad – with only two senior forward players available, Kane and the 18-year-old Lennart Karl.

Karl still almost won the game for the hosts, bending a shot from range against the top of the crossbar in stoppage time He might have many other chances to make himself the hero in the games to come. As will Kane, again and again. We will see quite how the immediate post-Ballon d’Or period will unfold. One of Kane’s key characteristics throughout his career has been his relentless availability, but part of his ascension to his best-ever self has been based on Kompany’s ability to rest his star turn and keep him fresh. With the current plethora of injuries, Danks is unlikely to have the same luxury.

It is impossible to talk about turning points in the season on Halloween. Yet Kane will be loading Bayern on his broad shoulders ever more than before, and Dortmund’s next challenge is to be brave enough to try to take advantage.

If Sebastian Hoeness and his Stuttgart team were going to lift themselves out of a crisis of confidence it was always going to be not by eking out a gritty result, but by blasting their way back to health, and that is what they did at Leverkusen, winning 4-2 in a fixture that has been one of the Bundesliga’s must-watch match-ups of recent seasons. For all their attacking punch, Hoeness and company arrived having lost four out of five on the back of some profligate finishing. Here they were clinical in a testy game against a Werkself team who had chances of their own. “Unfortunately, we can’t play Leverkusen 34 times,” lamented the Champions League joint top scorer Ermedin Demirovic, who scored twice. “They’re always heated and exciting matches because both teams play with attacking intent.”

Leipzig strolled to a 2-0 win at an impotent Schalke – still yet to score a home goal – before facing Manchester City, an important step to Martín Demichelis shoring up his position. The Norwegian winger Antonio Nusa, who scored one and made one, excelled.

Niclas Füllkrug was at it again for Werder Bremen, after an attempted midweek DFB Pokal rescue act at his old club Borussia Dortmund, scoring twice to bring Werder level before their hopes were dashed by a late Marcel Sabitzer winner. #845. How Paul Bettany Popped 10 Eye Blood Vessels While Filming VisionQuest

Paul Bettany revealed that scary ordeal he faced while filming the Disney+ series VisionQuest as he popped 10 blood vessels in his eye.

Paul Bettany has, quite literally, seen better days on Marvel sets.

Nearly two decades after joining the superhero franchise, the actor admitted filming his new TV series VisionQuest led to a pretty jarring injury—one that required no high-flying stunts. As he revealed, he accidentally popped 10 blood vessels in his eye while shooting a particularly harrowing scene for the new Marvel series.

“I was pretending to have a device on my head that is doing something to my brain,” Bettany recalled on the Oct. 29 episode of Jimmy Kimmel Live!, “and I was just wildly overacting.”

But because the 55-year-old was so dilated in, he ended up blowing out the vessels in his eye, quipping, “I mean, it was a lesson in less is more.”

Host Jimmy Kimmel pulled out a photo of Bettany from the set, showing just how bloody his left eye looked, adding, “I'm impressed when actors can cry on command, you’re actually able to pop your eye on command.”

But it was less than a perfect vision for the production team. The injury took about two weeks to fully heal, at which point they’d still had to continue on with filming VisionQuest, in which Bettany—who shares kids Stellan, 23, and Agnes, 15, as well as stepson Kai, 29, with wife Jennifer Connelly—reprises his role as Vision.

“I think it must have cost production so much to take it out,” Bettany considered, with Kimmel noting that they “had to do their magic and fix it.”

“I mean, the irony is the actor playing Vision is kind of myopic,” Bettany continued of his own nearsightedness. “I can’t see a thing when I take my glasses off.”

He added with a laugh, “Which is great depending on the actor.”

Luckily, VisionQuest kept him booked and busy in England, working alongside costars James Spader, Ruaridh Mollica, Emily Hampshire and more. Although, he was perhaps too busy, even for Vision’s epic Mindspace.

"I'm not complaining about the amount of work," Bettany shared with E! News in October, "but there are so many pages to get through in a day that you find yourself spending a lot of time working on scenes at night, and I found it really difficult to wind down at the end of the day."

Of course, he was truly bewitched by the opportunity to bring a new version of Vision to life almost 20 years after he joined the Marvel Universe as J.A.R.V.I.S. in 2008’s Iron Man.

"It was an amazing experience," he beamed, also teasing, "You're getting really well paid for it, and that's great."
